taxonomicNotes: The taxonomy of sea lions in New Zealand (Phocarctos) and Australia (Neophoca) was confused until it was resolved in a paper by King (1960).

There are two subspecies of the water vole: Arvicola sapidus sapidus (Miller, 1908) and Arvicola sapidus tenebricus (Miller, 1908). A. s. sapidus is present in Portugal and southern Spain, while A. s. tenebricus occurs in France and northern Spain. A. s. tenebricus is dark to reddish brown, while the coat of A. s. sapidus is generally lighter and more yellowish.
Two subspecies are recognized by Wilson and Reeder (2005): N. g. goral, and N. g. bedfordi.

Grubb (2005) recognized four subspecies: O. n. nivicola, O. n. borealis, O. n. kodarensis, and O. n. koriakorum. However, many Russian authors recognize a different set of subspecies: O. n. nivicola Eschscholtz, 1929 (Kamchatka); O. n. borealis Severtzov, 1873 (Taimyr); O. n. alleni Matsche, 1907 (East Siberia, Yablonovy and Stanovoy Ridges, to Verkhoyansky Ridge in the north); O. n. lydekkeri Kowarzik, 1913 (northeastern Siberia, from Lena River in the west to Stanovoy Ridge in the east, and Verkhoyansky Ridge in the south); and O. n. koriakorum Tschernyavsky, 1962 (Chukchi Peninsula and Koryak District) (K. Tsytsulina pers. comm.). Clearly subspecific taxonomy remains uncertain.

Groves (2001) and Meijaard and Groves (2002a, b) proposed to upgrade the three extant subspecies of Babyrousa to species level: B. celebensis from northern Sulawesi; B. togeanensis from the Togian islands; and B. babyrussa from Buru and the Sula Islands. A single skull from central Sulawesi may or may not represent the species known otherwise only as a subfossil from the southern peninsula, B. bolabatuensis. The taxonomic identity of the individuals from central, eastern and southeastern Sulawesi was left undecided. Until further studies have brought clarity all individuals occurring on Sulawesi, Muna, Buton and Lembeh are treated as Babyrousa celebensis.

Neas and Hoffmann (1987) recognized four subspecies: B. t. bedfordi, B. t. taxicolor, B. t. tibetana, and B. t. whitei. This taxonomy seems to be accepted by both western (Grubb 2005) and Chinese scientists (Wang et al. 1997, Zheng et al. 2003). In a recent analysis of the mtDNA control region, Li et al. (2003) identified three clades that corresponded generally with the three Chinese subspecies sampled.

There has been disagreement in the current taxonomy of Naemorhedus and Capricornis (Groves and Grubb 1985, Soma et al. 1987, Groves and Shields 1996) and is in need of revision. Recent genetic evidences have supported that Capricornis swinhoei is a distinct species from Capricornis crispus (Chang 2002, Min et al. 2004). Taxonomy of serows is not completely resolved; descriptions, range maps, and assessments of conservation status in the literature vary because sources differ on nomenclature and specific/subspecific status of the various taxa. Here, we follow the taxonomy of Wilson and Reeder, 3rd edition (2005). Thus, we recognize six species of Capricornis: • C. crispus (Japanese Serow, restricted to Japan) • C. milneedwardsii (Chinese Serow, but also occurring in southeast Asian countries) • C. rubidus (Red Serow, restricted to Myanmar) • C. sumatraensis (Sumatran Serow, in Indonesia, Malaysia and southern Thailand) • C. swinhoei (Formosan Serow, restricted to Taiwan, Province of China) • C. thar (Himalayan Serow, along the Himalayan range) The genus Naemorhedus is recognized as referring to gorals. Note that this taxonomy differs from that of Wilson and Reeder, 2nd edition (1993), that of the 2007 IUCN Red List (IUCN 2007), as well as that adopted by the IUCN Caprinae Specialist Group (Shackleton 1997). Additionally, most Chinese sources consider serows in China as being N. sumatraensis (e.g., Wang 1998, Wang 2002).
Sarcophilus laniarius has also been used recently in light of comparisons between a fossil specimen, S. laniarius (named prior to the naming of S. harrisii), and the extant species (Werdelin 1987).

Generally the generic name Cynocephalus is used, though Groves (2005) use the genus name Galeopterus. There is sometimes confusion between this species and the Giant Flying Squirrel (Boeadi pers. comm.).

This species was placed in family Dicotylidae by Jones et al. (1992) and in Tayassuidae by Grubb (2005). The appropriate generic name has been debated. It was placed in genus Dicotyles by some authors, the genus Pecari by Grubb (1993, 2005), and the genus Tayassu by Jones et al. (1992). MtDNA data support the recognition of three genera of extant peccaries: Catagonus, Pecari, and Tayassu, with this species in the genus Pecari (Theimer and Keim 1998, Gongora and Moran 2005). DNA studies suggest that P. tajacu may consist of at least two major clades or lineages comprising specimens from North/Central and South America (Gongora et al. 2006, 2011) with structural chromosomal differences (Gongora et al. 2000, Adega et al. 2006). Additional studies are needed to clarify whether intra and/or inter-specific genetic and chromosomal variation is occurring within this species.

Feldhamer et al. (1988) and Geist (1998) included Dama mesopotamica in this species, though it was regarded as a separate species from D. dama by Haltenorth (1959), Ferguson et al. (1985), Uerpmann (1987), and Harrison and Bates (1991). We follow Pitra et al. (2004) in treating D. mesopotamica as a separate species, based on that major study on the evolution and phylogeny of Old World deer.
Coelops hirsutus was previously considered a subspecies of Coelops robinsoni (Corbet and Hill 1992), however, we follow L. Heaney (pers. comm. 2007) in considering it to be a distinct species.
Generic synonyms = Galeopithecus, Galeopterus.

Atelocynus is a monotypic genus. The species has formerly been placed in the genera Lycalopex, Cerdocyon, and Dusicyon. Phylogenetic analysis has shown Atelocynus microtis to be a distinct taxon most closely related to another monotypic Neotropical canid genus, Speothos.

The Nilgiri Tahr was first described by Gray from a drawing and notes of General Hardwicke, and they were said to have been sent from Nepal and from Chittagong. However, it has hitherto only been found on the Neelgherry and adjacent hills, extending south along the Western Ghats nearly to Cape Comorin. The specific name given by Gray was the Tamul, word for rock or precipice goat. It was called Ibex by sportsmen in Madras (Jerdon, 1874).  Later, Rice, (1984) provided a detailed description on the taxonomic history of Tahr. The Nilgiri Tahr was first named Kemas hylocrius by (Ogilby, 1838). Based on molecular phylogenetic analysis, Ropiquet and Hassanin (2005) proposed the name Nilgiritragus hylocrius for the species as it is claimed that the three species of Tahr (Himalayan, Arabian and Nilgiri) have had different lineages.We follow Ropiquet and Hassanin (2005)in removing this species from the genus Hemitragus, and placing it in the monotypic genus Nilgiritragus, based on analyses of four molecular markers. No subspecies are recognized.

Phipps (1774) first described the Polar Bear as a distinct species and named it Ursus maritimus. Other names were suggested including Thalassarctos, Thalarctos, and Thalatarctos. Erdbrink (1953) and Thenius (1953) ultimately settled on Ursus (Thalarctos) maritimus because of interbreeding between Brown Bears (Ursus arctos) and Polar Bears in zoos. Based on the fossil record, Kurtén (1964) recommended the Phipps (1774) name Ursus maritimus, which was promoted by Harington (1966), Manning (1971) and Wilson (1976) and is used today (see DeMaster and Stirling 1981, Amstrup 2003, Wilson and Reeder 2005).
Groves in Wilson and Reeder (1993) treats this as a synonym under M. murinus. There is a problem with the typification of this taxon.

taxonomicNotes: It is doubtful that the current taxonomy provides a true picture of the diversity of the genus Aotus. Ruiz-Herrera et al. (2005) reported that cytogenetic studies have characterized 18 different karyotypes with diploid numbers ranging from 46 to 58 chromosomes. The taxonomy of the night monkeys essentially follows the revision by Hershkovitz (1983), with some modifications for the Colombian and Central American forms. Reviewing the entire taxonomy and distributions of the night monkeys, Aotus, Ford (1994) carried out multivariate analyses of craniodental measures and pelage patterns and colour, and also took into consideration chromosomal data and blood protein variations. Ford (1994) concluded that there was “good support” for just two species north of the Río Amazonas: A. trivirgatus (Humboldt, 1812) east and north of the Rio Negro, and the polymorphic A. vociferans to the west of the Rio Negro. Aotus vociferans, as such, would include all the forms north of the Río Amazonas/Solimões in Brazil (west of the Rio Negro), Peru, Colombia and Ecuador, and in the Chocó, northern Colombia and Colombian Andes, and Panama: brumbacki, lemurinus, griseimembra, and zonalis. Hernández-Camacho and Cooper (1976) restricted both lemurinus (Colombian Andes, elevations from 1,000 to 1500 m up to 3,000–3,200 m) and griseimembra (northern lowlands, Santa Marta mountains, west to Río Sinú, Río San Jorge, lower Río Cauca and lowlands of middle and upper Río Magdalena) to Colombia, while recognizing the form zonalis as the night monkey of north-western Colombia (Chocó) and Panama. Hershkovitz (1983) recognized lemurinus and griseimembra as distinct, but considered them to be subspecies of a single species; he made no mention of the name zonalis, but as he ascribed Central American night monkeys to A. lemurinus lemurinus, by implication he was regarding it as a synonym of this latter form. Groves (2001) followed Hernández-Camacho and Cooper (1976) in recognizing zonalis as the form in Panama, and listed it as a subspecies of lemurinus along with griseimembra and brumbacki Hershkovitz, 1983. Defler et al. (2001) concluded that the karyotype of Aotus hershkovitzi Ramirez-Cerquera, 1983 (from the upper Río Cusiana, Boyacá, Colombia; 2n = 58) was in fact that of true lemurinus, and that the karyotypes which Hershkovitz (1983) had considered to be those of lemurinus were in fact of zonalis. Defler et al. (2001) and others (Defler 2003, 2004; Defler and Bueno 2003) concluded that Aotus lemurinus of Hershkovitz (1983) is in fact three karyotypically well-defined species, and that the night monkeys of the lowlands of Panama and the Chocó region of Colombia belong to the species A. zonalis, and those of the Magdalena valley to A. griseimembra, while those above altitudes of 1500m should correctly be referred to as A. lemurinus. For a review of the taxonomy of the night monkeys of Panama and northern Colombia see Rylands et al. (2006). Defler and Bueno (2007) discussed the karyology of the grey-necked night monkeys and reaffirmed the validity of A. brumbacki, A. griseimembra, A. lemurinus, A. trivirgatus, A. vociferans and A. zonalis.

(2005) reported that cytogenetic studies have characterised 18 different karyotypes with diploid numbers ranging from 46 to 58 chromosomes. The taxonomy of the night monkeys essentially followed the early revision by Hershkovitz (1983), with some modifications for the Colombian and Central American forms. Recent molecular studies have made valuable contributions towards the understanding of night monkeys taxonomy and phylogenetic relations (Plautz et al.2009; Menezes et al. 2010). Hill (1962) and Stanyon et al. (1995) listed nine subspecies of the Red Howler Monkey (Alouatta seniculus): A. s. seniculus, A. s. arctoidea, A. s. stramineus, A. s. macconnelli, A. s. insulanus, A. s. amazonica, A. s. juara, A. s. puruensis, and A. s. sara. Alouatta seniculus sara is now recognized as a full species following Minezawa et al. (1985; see also Stanyon et al. 1995; Groves 2001, 2005).

Lawrance (1933) originally recognized the howlers from Belize, north and eastern Guatemala and the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, as to distinct taxa, within Aloutta palliata (A. p. pigra and A. p. luctuosa). Regarding A. p. pigra she mentioned “The differences, however, are so definite that they unquestionably indicate a separate subspecies; indeed, if it were not for the form found at Mountain Cow [A. p. luctuosa] which seems to be intermediate between this and typical A. p. palliata, one might be justified in calling it a distinct species” (Lawrance 1933, p. 334). Smith (1970) analysed pelage coloration patterns, and cranial and dental features of 238 specimens from across the range of A. palliata (including those studied by Lawrence, 1933) and compared them with a population sample of two sympatric forms of howler monkeys from the state of Tabasco, Mexico. He determined that the two (partially sympatric) forms from his sample constituted two well-differentiated species, and thus recommended A. pigra to be considered full species and separated from A. palliata. He considered A. p. luctuosa Lawrence, 1933 as junior synonym of A. pigra. Most authors have considered A. pigra as the single species of Black howler in Central America (e.g., Groves 2001, 2005; Rylands et al. 2006). Napier (1976) discussed that A. pigra was in fact A. villosa (Gray 1845), and Brandon-Jones (2006) argued that Alouatta pigra Lawrence, 1933 is a junior synonym. However, due to the poor condition of the type specimen of A. villosa, the lack of compelling evidence (genetic or otherwise) to ensure that this is in fact the same taxon as A. pigra, and in pro of taxonomic stability, Cortés-Ortiz et al. (2015a) continue to call this taxon A. pigra until further studies are completed. Using mtDNA markers, Cortés-Ortiz et al. (2003) confirmed that A. palliata and A. pigra comprise reciprocally monophyletic groups, justifying their separation into distinct species. Nonetheless, as pointed out by Cortés-Ortiz et al. (2015a) “the validity of A. pigra luctuosa from the Cayo District in Belize has yet to be evaluated with genetic data.”

The taxonomy of spider monkeys (Ateles spp.) is based on Kellogg and Goldman´s (1944) seminal review, and more recently complemented by morphological and molecular analysis of Froehlich et al. (1991), Collins and Dubach (2000), Nieves et al. (2005) and Morales-Jimenez et al. (2015). In all studies, brown spider monkeys (Ateles hybridus I. Geoffroy, 1829) form a monophyletic clade, justifying full species status following the molecular studies conducted by Collins (1999) and Collins and Dubach (2000). These studies found that brown spider monkeys form an ancient clade within the spider monkeys, separated from white-bellied spider monkeys (Ateles belzebuth) approximately 3 mya. This classification was reinforced by Nieves et al. (2005) using chromosomal and molecular markers. Hernández-Camacho and Defler (1989) and Defler (2004) argued for the validity of two distinct forms: brunneus Gray, 1872 from the western bank of the Magdalena River, and hybridus from the eastern bank of the Magdalena River in Colombia and Venezuela. Nonetheless, recent molecular studies using two mitochondrial markers suggest that there has been substantial gene flow between both populations and that both taxa do not represent monophyletic clades (Link et al. 2015). Thus, brown spider monkeys are currently considered a single taxon without subspecific divisions.

Based on a multi-locus phylogeny and a biogeographic analysis, Buckner and collaborators (2014) divided the genus Saguinus into two: the small-bodied tamarins Leontocebus, and the large-bodied tamarins Saguinus. As the golden-mantle saddleback tamarin is a small-bodied tamarin, its current genus is Leontocebus. Hershkovitz (1977) regarded this species as a subspecies of L. fuscicollis. Thorington (1988) concluded that the form tripartitus occurs on the right bank of the lower Río Napo where it would be sympatric with L. lagonotus (also previously regarded as a subspecies of L. fuscicollis) and, consequently, that it was a distinct species. However, there is still no evidence that it is actually sympatric with L. lagonotus. Rylands et al. (1993, 2000, 2011) and Groves (2001, 2005) listed it as a species, but a re-evaluation of the evidence for its distribution indicates that both Hershkovitz (1977) and Thorington (1988) may have been wrong (Heymann 2000; Rylands et al. 2010.), and sympatry between L. lagonotus and L. tripartitus has yet to be confirmed.

Saguinus n. graellsi is listed as a full species by Hernández-Camacho and Cooper (1976) and Defler (1994), on the basis that it is sympatric with a population of S. nigricollis in the region of Puerto Leguízamo in southern Colombia. Hernández-Camacho and Defler (1991) listed it as a subspecies of S. nigricollis, agreeing with Hershkovitz (1977). It was listed as a distinct species by Groves (2001, 2005) following the supposition of its sympatry with S. n. nigricollis. However, Defler (2003, 2004) has indicated that the occurrence of S. n. nigricollis north of the Rio Putumayo is doubtful. Based on a multi-locus phylogeny and a biogeographic analysis, Buckner and collaborators (2014) divided the genus Saguinus into two: the small-bodied tamarins Leontocebus, and the large-bodied tamarins Saguinus; this species belongs to the small-bodied tamarins (Leontocebus).

Formerly this species was in the genus Callithrix (see Rylands et al. 1993, 2000, 2008). Groves (2001, 2005) lists this species as Callithrix (Mico) leucippe.It is similar to Mico argentatus, predominantly white, but with tail and feet pale gold. The face and ears are largely unpigmented (Hershkovitz 1977). The taxonomy here follows Rylands (2012).

Formerly in the genus Callithrix (see Rylands et al. 1993, 2000, 2008). Groves (2001, 2005) lists this species as Callithrix (Mico) intermedius. Mico intermedius is similar to M. melanurus by the distinct pale thigh stripe, similarly coloured hindquarters, dark crown (just a little paler than melanurus), but lacks the ear-tuft (it has a rudimentary tuft from only behind the pinna and not the well-developed tuft from within and around the pinna as in humeralifer). The face is variably depigmented (some individuals have quite dark-greyish faces), the forequarters are paler, and varying parts of the tail are pale off-white rather than black (Hershkovitz 1977).

Formerly this species was in the genus Callithrix (see Rylands et al. 1993, 2000, 2008). Groves (2001, 2005) lists this species as Callithrix (Mico) nigriceps.This marmoset is darker than Mico emiliae, described by Vivo (1985) from adjacent Rondônia, but differs in the pigmentation of face and ears, pheomelanisation of the forelimbs, mantle and ventrum, a brown rather than grey dorsum, an orange to russet colouration of the posterior limbs, and pale hips and upper thighs (Ferrari 2008).Alperin (1995) argued that Mico nigriceps (Ferrari and Lopes 1992) and “Mico emiliae” from Rondônia belong to the same species.This work follows Rylands (2012).

The lion tamarins, Leontopithecus spp., are listed as separate species following Della Serra (1951), Rosenberger and Coimbra-Filho (1984), Snowdon et al. (1986), Mittermeier et al. (1988), Natori (1989) and Rylands et al. (1993). Leontopithecus chrysopygus and L. chrysomelas have been listed as subspecies of L. rosalia by Coimbra-Filho (1969), Coimbra-Filho and Mittermeier (1972, 1973), Hershkovitz (1977), Mittermeier and Coimbra-Filho (1981), Forman et al. (1986) and Seuánez et al. (1988), the latter two publications on the basis of identical chromosome morphologies. Coimbra-Filho (1990) has suggested that L. caissara was a subspecies of L. chrysopygus, which was not supported neither morphologically (Burity et al. 1999) nor molecularly (Perez-Sweeney et al. 2008). A molecular phylogeny recovered three obvious clades: L. chrysomelas, L. caissara and L. chrysopygus / L. rosalia, where L. chrysomelas is the first to diverge from the other three (Perez-Sweeney et al. 2008). Here we follow the taxonomy proposed by Rylands (2012).

Saimiri vanzolinii Ayres 1985 was described based on 13 specimens collected at the confluence of the Solimões and Japurá rivers and deposited in the Museum of Zoology at the University of São Paulo. The type locality is the northern shore of Lake Mamirauá, Amazonas, Brazil. Ayres (1985) allocated S. vanzolinii in the species group "Saimiri boliviensis" (Roman group), based on the taxonomic arrangement of Hershkovitz (1984). Saimiri vanzolinii was referred by Hershkovitz (1987) as a subspecies of S. boliviensis. Although no specimen was examined, Costello et al. (1993), based on the data described by Ayres (1985), considered S. vanzolinii as a junior synonym of S. sciureus. All subsequent authors followed Ayres (1985), considering S. vanzolinii as a valid species. Lynch Alfaro et al. (2015) analysed biogeographical and mitochondrial molecular data for the genus and concluded that S. vanzolinii is a valid species. More recently, Mercês (2018) performed an extensive morphological review of museum specimens of Saimiri species from throughout the Amazon basin; she also employed RAD-seq to sequence nuclear genomic markers to construct a Saimiri phylogeny. The nuclear genetic and morphological analyses by Mercês (2018) both provide strong evidence to place Saimiri vanzolinii as a distinct taxon and the sister species to Saimiri boliviensis.

Saimiri taxonomy follows Hershkovitz (1984) and Groves (2001, 2005). An alternative taxonomy is presented by Thorington Jr. (1985) as follows: S. sciureus sciureus (includes the forms albigena, macrodon, and ustus recognized by Hershkovitz, [1984]), S. sciureus boliviensis (includes the forms pluvialis Lönnberg, 1940 and jaburuensis Lönnberg, 1940 recognized by Hershkovitz [1987]), S. sciureus cassiquiarensis, S. sciureus oerstedii (includes the form citrinellus recognized by Hershkovitz [1984]), and S. madeirae (given as a junior synonym of S. ustus by Hershkovitz [1984]). Hernández-Camacho and Defler (1989) recognize S. sciureus caquetensis Allen 1916, given as a junior synonym of S. sciureus macrodon by Hershkovitz (1984). Costello et al. (1993) argued for the recognition of just two species: S. sciureus in South America, and S. oerstedii in Panama and Costa Rica. Boinski and Cropp (1999) using two nuclear genes (IRBP and ZFX) and one mitochondrial (D-Loop) strongly support the Hershkovitz (1984) taxonomy, advocating four distinct species: Saimiri sciureus, S. boliviensis, S. oerstedii and S. ustus. See Rylands et al. (2006) for a discussion of the taxonomy of the Central American squirrel monkeys.

There is a single record of a hybrid Red-shanked Douc (Pygathrix nemaeus) X Grey-shanked Douc (P. cinerea) in northeastern Cambodia (Rawson and Roos 2008). Current knowledge of the zones of transition between the three douc taxa is unclear, with limited information mostly based on brief field views (Timmins and Duckworth 1999, Nadler et al. 2004, Rawson and Roos 2008). There may be a zone in Viet Nam with sympatry (and possibly hybridization) between the three taxa (Lippold et al. 2011). Both Black-shanked Douc (P. nigripes) and Grey-shanked Douc were previously considered conspecific with Red-shanked Douc

In the past this taxon has been considered either a subspecies of Pygathrix nemaeus, or a hybrid of P. nemaeus and P. nigripes (Nadler 1995). Other studies on the genetics of doucs show that P. cinerea and P. nemaeus are sister taxa (Roos and Nadler 2001). There is strong evidence that this taxon hybridizes with Red-shanked Doucs (P. nemaeus) in a small sympatric distribution area of Quang Nam Province (Nadler 1997) and possibly in northeast Cambodia (Rawson and Roos 2008).

Monotypic. Show wide variation in coat colouration across their distribution but little genetic variation. Semnopithecus entellus sport the ‘Northern Type’ tail carriage, looped in the front. The tail either touches the back or falls on either side of the body.

This taxon was formerly considered a subspecies of Semnopithecus entellus. Recent investigations by Brandon-Jones seemed to indicate the S. hypoleucos population as part of S. dussumieri (Molur et al. 2003, Brandon-Jones 2004). Some experts believe this species to be merely a natural hybrid between Nilgiri Langur (Trachypithecus johnii) and S. dussumieri (Molur et al. 2003). Recent papers by Nag et al. (2011, 2014) and Ashalakshmi et al. (2014) recognizes S. hypoleucos as a distinct species with three recognized subspecies achates, iulus, and hypoleucos. A fourth subspecies aeneas after Pocock (1939) and Hill (1939) is also recognized.

This taxon was formerly considered a subspecies of Semnopithecus entellus. Groves (2001) and Brandon-Jones (2004) consider S. hector as a separate species with an extensive distribution through the juxta-Himalayan stretch, from Nepal through to India. Genetic studies might suggest further revision.

This taxon was formerly considered a subspecies of S. entellus.  The other two species lania and achilles described by Elliot (1909) and Pocock (1928), respectively are considered junior synonyms of Semnopithecus schistaceus by Groves (2001), as first postulated by Napier (1985).

Semnopithecus priam is here provisionally treated as a polytypic species including two recognized subspecies: S. p. priam and S. p. thersites (Brandon-Jones 2004, Groves 2005). However, limited evidence suggests that there are consistent differences between the two taxa, which may necessitate recognition of the two forms as distinct species (C. Groves pers. comm.). Recent publication by Name et al. (2011, 2014) and Ashalakshmi et al. (2014) delineates S. prima into two subspecies in southern India, viz., S. p. anchises, S. p. priam, and the Sri Lankan population as S. p. thersites.

This taxon was formerly considered a subspecies of Semnopithecus entellus (Molur et al. 2003).Pocock described the species in 1928 as Pithecus entellus ajax. In his 1939 review, W.C.O. Hill subsumed the taxon as a subspecies of S. schistaceus. Brandon-Jones (2004) followed with designating ajax as a subspecies of entellus. Within the group, at a same place fur coloration might change based on age and hierarchy, for example subadults fur is slightly whiter than an adult which is greyish but this needs to be studied further.

authority: Geissmann, Ngwe Lwin, Saw Soe Aung, Thet Naing Aung, Zin Myo Aung, Tony Htin Hla, Grindley & Momberg, 2011
taxonomicNotes: This is a recently described species of Snub-nosed Monkey from the high altitudes of northeastern Kachin state, northeastern Myanmar. Descriptions are based on a skin and skulls of four specimens obtained from local hunters. The new species is geographically isolated from other Snub-nosed Monkeys and separated from them by two major barriers the Mekong and the Salween (Thanlwin) rivers. It is closely related to Rhinopithecus bieti
Groves in Wilson and Reeder (1993) also treats this as a distinct species but under the genus Pygathrix. There is now good support to keep it in Rhinopithecus see Novak (1999).
This species was formerly considered to be in the genus Pygathrix.

Grubb et al. (2003) list two subspecies: Colobus satanas satanas from Bioko, and C. s. anthracinus from the mainland.Groves (2001, 2007) listed Colobus satanas anthracinus from Gabon (see Gautier-Hion et al. 1999) as a junior synonym of Colobus satanas (which occurs on Bioko Island). Groves (2005) and Grubb et al. (2003), however, listed it as a valid subspecies. Oates et al. (2000) found that the loud calls (roar pulse rate) of the two forms were significantly distinct (lower in C. s. satanas).

Booth (1954), Oates and Trocco (1983), Groves et al. (1993), Groves (2001) and Grubb et al. (2003) considered Dollman’s Black-and-White Colobus monkey, Colobus polykomos dollmani Schwarz, 1927, from areas between the Sassandra and Bandama Rivers in Western Côte d’Ivoire to be a hybrid of C. vellerosus × C. polykomos. Groves (2001, 2005, 2007) and Grubb et al. (2003) listed dollmani as a junior synonym of C. vellerosus. The question of the validity or otherwise of this form was raised by Gonedelé Bi et al. (2006) who, carried out surveys in 2003–2004 in three forest reserves and Marahoué National Park in search of Colobus polykomos dollmani between the Sassandra and Bandama Rivers and found just one group in Bolo Forest Reserve. But reviewing the evidence, Oates and McGraw (2009) opined that dollmani is a Colobus polykomos x Colobus vellerosus hybrid and should not be considered as a subspecies. Gonedelé Bi et al. (2014) subsequently conducted a survey in 2012 in the same region, but Bolo-Dassiéko-Niégré complex had been converted into a cocoa plantation. They found one group in Grébouo I Forest Grove, which is in close proximity to Bolo, where they found that the monkeys had a similar pelage as Colobus vellerosus, but in one vocal aspect, they were similar to Colobus polykomos. However, modest vocal data analysed by these authors produced more complex results. In one parameter (duration), the roar was similar to Colobus vellerosus; whereas it was more similar to Colobus polykomos than to Colobus vellerosus in the number of roars or subunit calls. Hence, Gonedelé Bi et al. (2014) were reluctant to draw definitive conclusions based on vocalisations.

Two subspecies are recognised: Cercopithecus petaurista petaurista to the east and C. p. buettikoferi to the west of the Cavally River on the Liberia-Côte d’Ivoire border (Oates 2011). This species belongs to the Cercopithecus cephus group.
Grubb et al. (2003) and Groves (2005) both recognise two subspecies: Cercopithecus erythrotis camerunensis (from between the Cross/Benue and Sanaga Rivers), and C. e. erythrotis (endemic to Bioko).
Groves (2001) and Grubb et al. (2003) recognize two subspecies: Cercopithecus erythrogaster erythrogaster and C. e. pococki. It belongs to the Cercopithecus cephus species group.
Monotypic species. It belongs to the Cercopithecus mona superspecies.
Kingdon (1997), Grubb et al. (2003), Groves (2005), and Cords and Sarmiento (2013) recognise five subspecies: C. a. ascanius, C. a. atrinasus, C. a. katangae, C. a. schmidti and C. a. whitesidei.

This species hybridizes with Macaca ochreata, M. maura and M. hecki in areas where their ranges overlap (Groves 2001). Molecular research did not find evidence that the so-called "Balantak Macaque" from the Togean Islands constitutes a distinct species, but it did indicate that the western and eastern populations are genetically distinct, and therefore, should be managed separately  (Evans et al. 2001).
Several subspecies have been recognized (Groves 2005), although Groves (2001) treated the species as monotypic. No subspecies are evaluated here, pending a revision of the taxon.

This species was once considered a subspecies of Macaca nigra. It is believed to hybridize with M. nigra on the western side of Mount Padang, and with M. hecki east of the Bolango River and near Bolaangitang (Groves 2001). In 1969, J. Fooden found substantial difference between M. nigra and M. nigrescens to classify each as a separate species. There were no intergradations found then. In 1980, Groves saw intergradations in the ‘zone of intergradation’ between M. nigra and M. nigrescens on the western tip of Bogani Nani Wartabone (formerly Dumoga Bone) National Park in the downstream region of Onggak Dumoga River, therefore placing M. nigrescens as subspecies of nominate M. nigra. Corbett and Hill (1992), in the review of The Mammals of the Indomalayan Region, followed Groves’ 1980 classification scheme. However, in 2001 Groves reviewed the classification, readdressing the previous schemes and redressing M. nigra and M. nigrescens. Despite the genetic and morphological similarity, the macaques are considered distinct and as members of the silenus group of macaques.

Morphology, genetics and taxonomic variation in northeastern Indian macaques, including this taxon, is very poorly known (Sinha et al. 2006a, Chakraborty et al. 2007). Further taxonomic research is required in order to better understand its relationship to Macaca assamensis and M. thibetana.

This species hybridizes with Macaca tonkeana and possibly with M. nigrescens in areas where their ranges overlap (Bynum 1995). These hybrid zones, however, appear to be disappearing owing to human encroachment (M. Richardson pers. comm.). Mitochondrial DNA studies suggest sister relationship with M. nemestrina, M. nigrescens, M. nigra, and M. tonkeana. (Evans et al. 1999)

Siberut Macaques were initially thought to be a subspecies of the southern pigtail macaque - Macaca nemestrina pagensis (Fooden 1975) and then of the Mentawai/Pagai macaque of the southern Mentawai Islands - M. pagensis siberu (Fuentes and Olson 1995). More recently, genetic and morphological studies led to their classification as a distinct species (Kitchener & Groves 2002, Roos et al. 2003), showing that this primate is more closely related to M. nemestrina on Sumatra and Malaysia than to M. pagensis on the neighboring Mentawai Islands (Ziegler et al. 2007, Richter et al. 2013). Along with M. pagensis, M. leonina, M. nemestrina and M. silenus, it belongs to the ‘silenus group’ (Roos et al. 2003).

Belongs to the fascicularis species group alongside Macaca mulatta, M. fascicularis and M. fuscata. A drop in sea level and glacial advances c.300,000 years ago is said to have brought the species’ progenitor to the island from eastern mainland of Asia. Molecular genetic studies by Jui-Hua Chu and colleagues suggest the divergence of M.cyclopsis and M.fuscata from mainland M. mulatta to be of 0.38-0.44 million years ago.

Until relatively recently, Macaca pagensis included M. siberu (Roos et al. 2003). It is now considered a separate species from M. siberu due to genetic and morphological difference. Earlier it was considered as a subspecies of M. nemestrina until established as a separate species.

Two distinct subspecies are recognized apart from the Macaca assamensis population that is endemic to and found in Nepal, and which is likely in some way distinct (Chalise pers. comm). The two subspecies, M. a. assamensis and M. a. pelops, respectively occupy adjacent areas to the southeast and east of the range of M. assamensis.This is member of sinica species group that includes M. sinica, M. radiata, M. thibetana. All members of sinica group are allopatric or parapatric, extending down south from Sri Lanka to eastern central China. The members of the group are characterized by a peculiar glans-penis, slender to the tip and 30 mm long. Two subspecies recognized: M. assamensis pelops and M. assamensis assamensis. Both the species differ in relative tail length of adult males. The Nepal form, different in colour and form could be a different subspecies.

Individuals with intermediate characteristics, presumably hybrids, have historically been seen along the border of this species' range and that of Macaca nigrescens (although this contact zone may no longer exist; Sugardjito et al. 1989). The zone of intergradation is the downstream region of the Onggak Dumoga River and Groves (1980) placed M. nigrescens as a subspecies of M. nigra. Despite the morphological and genetical similarity, M. nigra and M. nigrescens are still distinct and therefore classified as distinct species (Groves 2001). Macaca nigra belongs to the silenus group including M. pagensis, M. siberu, M. leonina, M. silenus, and M. nemestrina.

Aside from the two previously recognized forms, a third subspecies, M. s. opisthomelas, is also now also recognized by primate field biologists in Sri Lanka, which is assessed separately here. There is some inter-gradation between the three subspecies (Groves, 2001; Dittus, 2013).The taxonomy of Macaca sinica:The species belongs to the sinica group (Groves, 2001). Three subspecies are recognized and assessed here:Macaca sinica sinica (Linnaeus, 1771)Macaca sinica aurifrons (Pocock, 1931)Macaca sinica opisthomelas (Hill, 1942)In addition to the two previously recognized forms, a third subspecies, M. s. opisthomelas first described by Hill (1942), is confirmed by primate field biologists in Sri Lanka (Dittus 2013; Eisenberg and McKay 1970; Phillips 1935, 1980). It is a distinct phenotype apical in the higher elevations of the montane zone. It is not a type intermediate (in morphology or geographic distribution) between M. s. aurifrons and M. s. sinica as had been suggested by Brandon-Jones et al. (2004) and Groves (2001) following the suggestion by Fooden (1979). It was first assessed in 2003 (CAMP 2003, Molur et al. 2003, Dittus et al. 2008) and is updated here along with the other macaque subspecies. A fourth population M. s. longicaudata has been described by Deraniyagala (1965) but its status is uncertain and has been considered as a variant of M. s. sinica (Eisenberg and McKay, 1970).  There are some intergradations between the three subspecies where their respective areas of occupancy overlap (Groves, 2001).
Macaca silenus is a member of the silenus group. The other phylogenetic sister species in this group include M. leonina, M. siberu, M. nemestrina, M. pagensis and the seven Sulawesi species.

Two subspecies are recognized, distinguished on the grounds of both morphological (Macaca radiata radiata is dark bellied and M. r. diluta is pale bellied), and behavioural differences (females largely disperse between groups only in M. r. diluta, while males disperse in both the subspecies; M. Singh pers. comm.).

Mandrillus was regarded as a subgenus of Papio by Dandelot (in Meester and Setzer 1972) and Wolfheim (1983), but recent molecular and chromosomal analyses suggest that Mandrillus is closer to the terrestrial mangabeys Cercocebus spp. (Disotell 1993, Fleagle and McGraw 2002). Two genetically distinct populations have been noted, north and south of the Ogooué River (Telfer et al. 2003).

Formerly placed by some in the genus Papio (Wolfheim, 1983), genetic analyses shows Mandrillus is more closely related to Cercocebus than to Papio (Disotell et al. 1992, Disotell 1994); morphological research concurs (Fleagle and McGraw 1999, McGraw and Fleagle 2006).There are two subspecies: M. l. leucophaeus on the mainland, and M. l. poensis on Bioko (Zukowsky 1922). Grubb et al. (2003) commented that on present evidence the two forms appear very similar.

Formerly includes anubis, cynocephalus, papio, and ursinus, but see Jolly (1993), Kingdon (1997) and Groves (2001) and others who recognized these as distinct species (Grubb et al. 2003). The Arabian population was formerly recognised with the name arabicus Thomas, 1900. Recent studies demonstarted Arabian hamadryas baboons migrated naturally into Arabian Peninsula via land bridges that formed periodically during glacial maxima at the straits of Bab el Mandab in the southern Red Sea (Winney et al. 2004, Kopp et al. 2014).

This species was previously treated as a subspecies of Papio hamadryas, but now is considered a species (Kingdon 1997, Groves 2001, 2005, Grubb et al. 2003). There are some regional differences in morphology and pelage colour, but there are no currently recognised subspecies (Zinner 2013).Papio anubis hybridizes with P. cynocephalus in a broad clinal zone between Laikipia district to the northeast of Mont Kenya and the Lower Tana River near the Kenya coast. In that 200-km wide area, baboons are intermediate in appearance and are difficult to allocate to either species (Zinner 2013). Hybridization with P. papio is likely but has not been confirmed. Hybridization with Theropithecus gelada has been observed in the wild and even hybridization with White-naped Mangabeys (Cercocebus lunulatus) is suspected (R. Matsuda Goodwin pers. comm. 2020). According to a review presented by Zinner (2013), P. anubis from Eritrea and Ethiopia carry maternally inherited mitochondria that are closely related to P. hamadryas mitochondria and P. anubis in Kenya and Tanzania carry mitochondria closely related to P. cynocephalus mitochondria, indicating that male introgression by P. anubis might be the major form of hybridization.

This species was formerly placed in the genus Nasalis. Recent molecular analysis suggest a close relationship between Simias and Nasalis, however, current classification still places Simias concolor in its own genus (Whittaker et al. 2006). To date, two subspecies are recognised, primarily based on slight differences in pelage colouration: S. c. concolor, which is found in Indonesia on the islands of Sipora, North Pagai, as well as South Pagai, and S. c. siberu, which is exclusively found on the island of Siberut (Miller 1903, Chasen and Kloss 1927).

Machado (1969) revised the genus and clearly established the differences between Miopithecus talapoin and an unnamed species, later named by Kingdon (1997). The spelling ogouensis was used in the original description of the taxon and should therefore be retained, though it would have been preferable to have spelt it ogooueensis, because it is based on the River Ogooué (Grubb et al. 2003).

The taxonomy of Presbytis siamensis is disputed and has undergone several changes. It was formerly considered a subspecies of P. femoralis (e.g. Chasen 1940) or a subspecies of P. melalophos (e.g. Oates et al. 1994). Currently it is considered a species of its own (e.g. Brandon-Jones 1984; Groves 2001; Groves and Roos 2013; Roos et al. 2014), but there remains an urgent need to clarify the taxonomy and distribution of what is now considered P. siamensis, at both the species and subspecies levels (Groves and Roos 2013).

Currently, five sub-species are recognised on the IUCN Red List though the basis for this split appears to be arbitrary and all must thus be listed as DD. •      Presbytis rubicunda rubicunda •      Presbytis rubicunda rubida •      Presbytis rubicunda ignita •      Presbytis rubicunda chrysea •      Presbytis rubicunda carimatae Subspecies are disputed as there is much inter-gradation between them, as well as variation within them. The separation is to do with the shape of the crescent and the extent of the whorl on the forehead, and the extent of black(ish) hair around the hands and feet, for the separation of P. rubida and P. rubicunda. P. chrysea and P. ignita are more obviously different because of their hair colour, moving to orange-red upwards along the north-south gradient. P. carimatae has an orange nape. Most of the justification for this split is based on pelage rather than differences in call or genetic data. These morphological subspecies are currently not supported by genetic data.
Possibly referebale to P. comata.

All of the former subspecies of Presbytis melalophos are now recognised as distinct species. However, the species has colour morphs: the ‘foxy-red nobilis’, ‘less-reddish ferruginae’ and ‘golden buff aurata’, black chested, white tail tipped and the hands and feet black. A fourth form ‘fluvialtilis’ described in 1940 by N.F. Chasen of Palembang, Sumatra is also accounted for.
Presbytis potenziani is now monotypic and the former subspecies P. p. siberu is now a distinct species.
Semnopithecus frontatus S. Muller, 1838, Indonesia, south-eastern Borneo. Restricted by L. Medway in 1965 to south eastern Kalimantan, Murung and Pulu Lampy, near Banjarmasin, Pematang, Kuala.

This taxon was formerly considered a subspecies of Presbytis femoralis and P. melalophos. The number of subspecies is disputed. In addition to the two generally recognized forms (Presbytis chrysomelas chrysomelas and P. c. cruciger) there is an additional, isolated population found only in a small area of southeastern Sarawak (Betong, Saribas; Nimong; Batang Lupar) that probably represents an as yet undescribed subspecies (Groves 2001).
This species has been variously considered a subspecies of Presbytis siamensis, P. femoralis and P. melalophos.
Grubb et al. (2003) included this species in Cercocebus galeritus, but Groves (2005) and Kingdon (2001) considered it distinct.

Cercocebus chrysogaster is poorly known. There are no detailed studies of the species, which is documented by fewer than 20 specimens (Ehardt and Butynksi 2013). The species has alternately been assigned as a subspecies of Cercocebus agilis or Cercocebus galeritus but retained as a separate species by Groves (2005). The species range currently consists of two allopatric populations. The western population and eastern population are reported to have differences in pelage (Groves 1978). Photographs suggest that western animals are more brightly coloured than eastern animals (J. Hart unpublished data 2010). Occurrence of outliers in the original description of the species’ range may be attributed to records of captive animals that originated from other areas (Groves 1978, Gautier-Hion et al. 1999).

Grubb et al. (2003) treated this form as a subspecies of Cercopithecus aethiops, but it is here regarded as a distinct species, following Groves (2001, 2005) and it is now included in the genus Chlorocebus (Groves 2005, Groves and Kingdon 2013). However, because it appears to grade imperceptibly in the vervet (Chlorocebus pygerythrus) range in the northeastern, eastern and southeastern parts of its distribution, with no obvious barriers, the species’ classification is still considered problematic by some (Ansell 1978 in Sarmiento 2013 and see Sarmiento 2013 for full discussion). Generally considered monotypic, though this too requires further study.

A first comparison of the three major taxa of the Cercopithecus aethiops group, using electrophoretic polymorphism, concluded an intermediate status between subspecies and populations (Lucotte et al. 1982). The species was treated by Grubb et al. (2003) as a subspecies of C. aethiops, but here it is considered distinct. Grubb et al. (2003) retained this species in Cercopithecus, but here it is placed in Chlorocebus following Groves (2005) and Groves and Kingdon (2013).There is a slight north-to-south gradient with regard to sexual dimorphism (males larger in the north) and colour of dorsum, which is yellower in the northern popualtions (Galat et al. 2011, Galat & Galat-Luong 2013). In the Comoé-Leraba Hunting Reserve, some individuals look like C. tantalus monkeys (A. Galat-Luong pers. obs. 2003–2006). Some individuals on the west bank of the Volta River in Ghana carry C. tantalus mitochondrial haplotypes indicating possible (human induced) hybridization (Haus et al. 2013). Evidence for ancient hybridization between the two species has been found (Svardal et al. 2017).

Grubb et al. (2003) treated this taxon as a subspecies of C. aethiops, but it is here listed as a distinct species (see C. aethiops for further details). Kingdon (1997), Groves (2001, 2005) and Nakagawa (2013) include this taxon in Chlorocebus and recognise three subspecies: C. t. tantalus, C. t. budgetti and C. t. marrensis.

Mitochondrial DNA studies now classify Trachypithecus johnii and Trachypithecus vetlus under the genus Semnopithecus (Osterholz et al. 2008, Wang et al. 2012). Semnopithecus johnii hybridizes as a brown hybrid with Semnopithecus priam where they are parapatric.
There is some interbreeding of released Francois’ langurs with Trachypithecus leucocephalus south and east of the River Zuo in Guangxi, China (Groves 2001).

This taxon was formerly considered as a subspecies of Trachypithecus francoisi. The taxon was elevated to species level by Brandon-Jones (1984) and Groves (2001), the later conclusion being supported by molecular genetic studies (Roos 2003, 2004) and parasitological findings (May 1994).

This taxon, here considered monotypic, was regarded in the 1960s–1990s as conspecific with Trachypithecus francoisi (Steinmetz et al. 2011). A variety of later classifications have been suggested, all based on inadequate primary information for confidence in their value. For example, Roos et al. (2007) proposed the species T. laotum to contain also the subspecies T. l. hatinhensis (with T. [auratus] ebenus as provisionally synonymous with T. l. hatinhensis). It is here considered a distinct species (as per Roos et al. 2014), though its classification in relation to T. ebenus and T. hatinhensis cannot be resolved without additional primary information.

Mitochondrial DNA studies now classify Trachypithecus vetlus and Trachypithecus johnii under the genus Semnopithecus (Osterholz et al. 2008, Wang et al. 2012). Four subspecies of Semnopithecus vetulus are recognized, namely: vetulus, monticola, nestor, and philbricki. An additional subspecies, S. v. harti, is also recognized by some experts, but is here included as a synonym of S. v. philbricki (Groves 2001).Southern Purple Faced Langur, Semnopithecus vetulus vetulus (Erxleben 1777): Southwestern Sri Lanka in the Wet Zone, from Kalu Ganga (River) to Ranna in the south up to an elevation of 1,000 m.Highland Purple Faced Langur, Semnopithecus vetulus monticola (Kelaart, 1850): Central Sri Lanka (1,000-2,200 m).Western Purple Faced Langur, Semnopithecus vetulus nestor (Bennett, 1833): Western Sri Lanka in the Wet Zone North of Kalu Ganga (River), up to 1,000 m elevation.Northern Purple Faced Langur, Semnopithecus vetulus philbricki (Philips, 1927): Northern and Eastern Sri Lanka in the Dry Zone, up to 1,500 m.

Formerly considered comprising two subspecies, Trachypithecus poliocephalus poliocephalus Trouessart, 1911, and T. p. leucocephalus Tan, 1955 (Groves 2001, 2005; Roos et al. 2007), Groves (2007) and Nadler (2013a,b) considered leucocephalus to be a full species (Roos et al. 2014). Now, T. poliocephalus (formerly T. p. poliocephalus) is a monotypic species

This was formerly part of Semnopithecus cristatus, but it is not clear what the current concept includes. It may or may not have been partially included within Trachypithecus auratus cristatus, which is confined to Indonesia according to D. Brandon-Jones. Ardith Eudey (in litt. 2000) believes that he may have assigned the remainder of the species to T. obscurus.

Despite a confusing history of taxonomic classification (Khajuria and Agrawal 1979), a recent genetic study supports the classification of Trachypithecus barbei as a monotypic species distinct from the similar, and closely related, T. obscurus (Geissmann et al. 2004, Osterholz et al. 2008). Evidently, there are a few rather well-defined morphs associated with this species, though no actual subspecies. Two morphs are identified in this species namely the silvery argenteus and ashy-grey holotephreus. T. barbei is of the obscurus-group which includes T. obscurus, T. crepusculus and T. phayrei. It is sympatric with T. germaini.

Seven subspecies are currently recognized: Trachypithecus obscurus carbo, T. o. flavicauda, T. o. halonifer, T. o. obscurus, T. o. sanctorum, T. o. seimundi, and T. o. styx. It may be that the blackish insular subspecies (carbo, halonifer, seimundi, styx) represent a distinct taxon which has been entirely replaced on the mainland by the contrastingly toned T. obscurus.
Originally included in Trachypithecus pileatus, T. shortridgei was recognised as a separate species by Groves (2001).

Africa's most recently discovered (2003) and described (2006) genus of monkey (Davenport et al. 2006). Originally allocated to the genus Lophocebus (Jones et al. 2005), but later placed in the monotypic genus Rungwecebus by Davenport et al. (2006) on the basis of molecular and morphological data. The genus to which R. kipunji belongs was questioned by Ehardt and Butynski (2006), but considerable further evidence supports the phylogenetic position and taxonomic status of Rungwecebus (Olson et al. 2008, Roberts et al. 2009). The evolutionary implications of Rungwecebus being a sister taxon to Papio are considerable (Olson et al. 2008, Davenport 2013).

Groves (2005) listed this taxon as Galago gabonensis, but it is retained here in Sciurocheirus following Grubb et al. (2003). The undescribed form located in the area of Foret des Abeilles near Makande, Gabon (Ambrose 2003) is now described as S. makandensis (Ambrose 2013) and assessed separately.

Grubb et al. (2003) state that there might be more than two subspecies of Euoticus elegantulus, of which the form south of the Ogooue River has not yet been named. Taxonomy reviewed in Ambrose (2013).

First collected from sites in SE Tanzania (near Newala, Makonde Plateau, in 1953, and Rondo Plateau in 1955) and provisionally identified by R.W. Hayman (in litt.) as Demidoff’s galago Galago demidovii and later Galago demidovii orinus (Jenkins 1987, Honess 1996) due to its small size and morphology. First recognised and described as a species, based on differences in vocalisations and morphology by Honess and Bearder (1996) and subsequently accepted by Groves (2001) and Grubb et al. (2003).A phylogenetic analysis of the lorisiform primates by Pozzi et al. (2015) showed that Galagoides demidoff and G. thomasi comprise a clade entirely separate from the remaining species currently placed in the genus Galagoides: G. rondoensis, G. orinus, G. zanzibaricus, G. cocos and G. granti. This latter group is sister to Galago É. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire 1796, with the two lineages diverging about 15 mya, and has been attributed to a separate genus Paragalago Masters et al. 2017. Galagoides is now restricted to the western forms: demidoff (G. Fischer, 1806), thomasi (Elliot, 1907), and kumbirensis Svensson, Bersacola, Mills, Munds, Nijman, Perkin, Masters, Couette, Nekaris and Bearder, 2017.

Grubb et al. (2003) concluded that the correct Latin name for Demidoff’s galago was demidovii, as referred to in Fischer (1808), which was written in Latin with, consequently, the latinised name of Demidoff. The epithet demidovii was used by Oates (2011), Ambrose and Butynski (2013) and Nekaris (2013). Groves (2001), however, argued that demidoff, as written by Fischer (1806), was in fact being used as a Latin binomial, and was as such the correct name for this species. This was also argued by Jenkins (1987) and Kingdon (1997), and Masters and Couette (2015) who used the name demidoff. Jenkins et al. (2018) confirmed the validity of the name demidoff Fischer. 1806.Groves (2001, 2005) recognised six subspecies, evidently, as pointed out by Masters and Couette (2015), following the concept of geospecies proposed by Grubb (2006): the nominate subspecies in “West Africa”; the Calabar dwarf galago Galagoides demidoff murinus (Murray, 1859) in the Nigeria-Cameroon border region; the Bioko Dwarf Galago G. d. poensis (Thomas, 1904) from the island of Bioko; the Congo dwarf galago G. d. anomurus (de Pousargues, 1893) from between the Sanaga and Congo rivers; the Kasai dwarf galago G. d. phasma Cabrera and Ruxton, 1926, from the south of the Congo River; the Uele dwarf galago G. d. medius (Thomas, 1915) from the Uele-Ituri region; and an undescribed form from Lake Oku, Bamenda Highlands, Cameroon. Kingdon (1997, 2015) listed these subspecies, as did Ambrose and Butynski (2013), the latter authors considering them, however, to be “tentative and provisional” (p.460). Grubb et al. (2003) argued that Galagoides demidoff was best considered monotypic. Masters and Couette (2015) carried out a cranial and dental morphometric study of G. demidoff and G. thomasi. On the basis of this study, they found “slight but consistent morphological differences between G. demidoff and G. thomasi but could not validate the subspecies described for the former taxon” (p. 297). The Bioko form, G. d. poensis, is assessed as a separate subspecies, as is the nominate subspecies. The Bioko form, G. d. poensis, is assessed as a separate subspecies, as is the nominate subspecies.

This latter group is sister to Galago É. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire 1796, with the two lineages diverging about 15 mya, and has been attributed to a separate genus Paragalago Masters et al. 2017. Galagoides is now restricted to the western forms: demidoff (G. Fischer, 1806), thomasi (Elliot, 1907), and kumbirensis Svensson, Bersacola, Mills, Munds, Nijman, Perkin, Masters, Couette, Nekaris and Bearder (2017).

Following its description by Elliot (1907) G. thomasi was regarded a subspecies of G. demidovii until 1979 when Olson (1979) resurrected G. thomasi to a full species based on larger body size and morphology. Masters and Couette (2015) confirm that G. thomasi and G. demidovii are different species with significant interspecific differences in the size and proportions of the skulls. G. thomasi and G. demidovii are sympatric through much of their range.

Monotypic species. Recognized by Groves (2001, 2005), Grubb et al. (2003), Butynski and De Jong (2013), and Kingdon (2015).
The subpopulation on the Itombwe Massif (Democratic Republic of the Congo) appears to be different and may represent a distinct taxon (Bearder 1999, Omari et al. 1999, T. Butynski pers. obs. 1996).
Grubb et al. (2003) listed four subspecies: Galago senegalensis senegalensis; G. s. braccatus; G. s. dunni, and G. s. sotikae.

Grubb et al. (2003) separated out the form Otolemur monteiri as a distinct species. However, there is a wide area of overlap in the distribution of forms attributable to O. monteiri and O. crassicaudatus in Tanzania (Groves 2001). For the current assessment, O. monteiri is regarded as a subspecies of O. crassicaudatus based on information regarding its skull morphology (Masters and Lubinsky 1988) and karyotype (Masters 1986). Greater Galago subspecies show minor differences in skull size but not in proportions, while skulls of the two recognized Otolemur species can readily be distinguished on the basis of skull proportions. Otolemur crassicaudatus subspecies are defined mainly on pelage coloration, which is likely to be adapted to the foliage in which the animals rest during the day, rather than for specific-mate recognition. Hence, the subspecies that occupy dry forests in miombo woodlands (O. c. monteiri, O. c. argentatus) are pale in colour, while those from the dune forests of KwaZulu-Natal and the montane forests of Limpopo Province (O. c. crassicaudatus) are darker.
Four subspecies are recognized by Groves (2001), Grubb et al. (2003), and Harcourt and Perkin (2013): O. g. garnettii, O. g. panganiensis; O. g. lasiotis, and O. g. kikuyuensis.

This taxon is monotypic (Geissman et al. 2002; T. Geissmann pers. comm.). Although it as been suggested that there is evidence for two genetically distinct Javan gibbon populations (Andayani et al. 2001), a review of the molecular evidence and a comparison of morphological and vocal data casts doubt on this claim (Geissman et al. 2002, Dallmann and Geissmann 2009, T. Geissmann pers. comm.).

This species forms a narrow area of sympatry and hybridization with H. lar in Khao Yai National Park, Thailand (Brockelman 1978, Brockelman and Gittins 1984, Marshall and Brockelman 1986, Marshall and Sugardjito 1986), specifically in the headwaters of the Takhong-Mun-Mekong River system (W. Brockelman pers. comm.). Until at least 1925, an area of sympatry apparently existed in the region of Sriracha, about 80 km southeast of Bangkok. Therefore, a large zone of overlap in the distribution of the two species may originally have existed. In most parts of this hypothetical zone, gibbon habitat appears to have been destroyed, with the Khao Yai Park possibly representing the last remnant of the once large contact zone (Geissmann 1991).

This taxon was traditionally classified as a subspecies of H. agilis, but Groves (2001) proposed it be considered a distinct species based on diagnostic pelage characteristics. Subsequent cytogenetic and molecular genetic analyses confirm the separation between H. agilis on Sumatra and H. albibarbis on Borneo (Hirai et al. 2005, 2009). H. albibarbis hybridizes with H. muelleri in a wide area of central Borneo (Marshall and Sugardjito 1986; Mather 1992, 1999).

This species forms a narrow area of sympatry and hybridization with H. pileatus in Khao Yai National Park, central Thailand (Brockelman 1978; Brockelman and Gittins 1984; Marshall and Brockelman 1986; Marshall and Sugardjito 1986), and with H. agilis in northern Peninsular Malaysia (W. Brockelman pers. comm.). Until at least 1925, an area of sympatry apparently existed in the region of Sriracha, about 80 km southeast of Bangkok. Therefore, a large zone of overlap in the distribution of H. lar and H. pileatus may originally have existed. In most parts of this hypothetical zone, gibbon habitat appears to have been destroyed, with the Khao Yai Park possibly representing the last remnant of the once large contact zone (Geissmann 1991). These zones demonstrate that reproductive isolation between the species is incomplete, although they do not freely interbreed in the wild where they are in contact (Brockelman and Gittins 1984). The subspecies of Hylobates lar, although numerous and well-distributed latitudinally, are not highly distinct, in general. They are based largely on relatively minor body color variation and the degree of polychromatism of the fur (Brockelman 1985, 2004; Groves 2001; Woodruff 2005) The validity of H. l. yunnanensis as a subspecies is doubtful; it requires comparison with H. l. carpenteri (C. Groves and T. Geissmann pers. comm.). The only geographically well-separated subspecies is H. l. vestitus, which is found on Sumatra; despite its (relatively recent) isolation, however, it is not highly distinct phenotypically (W. Brockelman pers. comm.). The taxonomic status of all the H. lar subspecies, and specifically yunnanensis, requires further investigation.
Genetic and vocal data suggested little difference in population across the islands and, therefore, Hylobates klossii is considered monotypic.

There is debate as to the validity of the subspecies. The general consensus seems to be that this species is monotypic (Hirai et al. 2009; Roos et al. 2014), though some experts recognize two subspecies on Sumatra: H. a. agilis to the west, and H. a. unko to the east (these may possibly correspond with "mountain" and "lowland" forms, respectively). All this is not to be confused with the two main color morphs found throughout the species' range, though in general the pale morph is more common in the Barisan Range of Sumatra, while in the eastern lowlands and in the Malay Peninsula black predominates (Marshall and Sugardjito 1986).

The mainland (Symphalangus syndactylus continentis) and Sumatran (Symphalangus syndactylus syndactylus) forms have been considered distinct subspecies; however, no subspecies are recognized in the most recent Asian primate taxonomy by Roos et al. (2014).

This taxon is now considered monotypic; it was formerly considered conspecific with Hoolock leuconedys. The previous generic name, Bunopithecus, was changed by Mootnick and Groves (2005) to Hoolock (Haimoff et al. 1984).
This taxon is monotypic; it was formerly considered a subspecies of H. hoolock. The previous generic name, Bunopithecus, was changed by Mootnick and Groves (2005) to Hoolock (Haimoff et al. 1984).

Previously four subspecies were recognised (N. c. concolor, N. c. furvogaster, N. c. jingdongensis and N. c. lu) (Ma and Wang 1986), however N. c. furvogaster of south-western Yunnan, west of Mekong River and N. c. jingdonensis of west central Yunnan, China are now considered synonomous with the nominate form while N. c. lu is recognised as a valid subspecies (Thinh et al 2010a,b).

This taxon was variously considered a subspecies of N. concolor, N. leucogenys and N. gabriellae. It was believed that N. siki might be a natural hybrid of N. leucogenys and N. gabriellae but this is due to missing information in the past. Genetic and acoustic data clearly show that this taxon is a valid species (Thinh et al. 2010a, Thinh et al. 2010b, Thinh et al. 2011).The recent discovery of N. annamensis and the extended southward distribution of N. leucogenys have largely reduced the distribution of the species. The limits of distribution of this species are not finally settled, both with regards to N. annamensis in the south and N. leucogenys in the north. Similarly, phenotype information for the type locality of N. siki (Thua Luu, Thua Thien Hue province, central Viet Nam) is contradictory (Geissmann et al. 2000; Thinh et al. 2010b). Though the holotype represents N. siki morphologically, the type locality falls in the range of N. annamensis (Thinh et al. 2010a). Recent genetic data of the N. siki holotype clearly confirm that this specimen is N. siki (C. Roos pers. comm.). Unfortunately, information about whether Jean Delacour and Pierre Jabouille collected the specimen in the wild near Thua Luu or whether they obtained the gibbon at a market or from a poacher is not traceable. However, since Thua Luu is close to the coast and along the Vietnamese national railway line and the national road no. 1, and considering the morphology and genetic data of the holotype, the specimen most likely originated from a place other than Thua Luu.

This taxon was previously considered a subspecies of N. concolor (Groves 1972). The limits of the distribution of this species are from Ba River, 13°00’-13°10’N in Gia Lai and Phu Yen provinces and Sre Pok River in North to Nui Ong Nature Reserve in 11°01’N in Binh Thuan Province in South, and South East Cambodia (East of Mekong River). Populations that occurs south of Thach Han River in central Viet Nam, southern Lao and northeastern Cambodia differ in their song from N. gabriellae in the south (e.g. Konrad and Geissmann 2006) and was separated from N. gabriellae as a distinct species, namely N. annamensis (Thinh et al. 2010).

Previously, Nomascus hainanus was variously considered either a species in its own right or as a subspecies of N. concolor or N. nasutus; it is here recognized as a distinct species based on molecular, vocalization and pelage differences (Geissmann et al. 2000; Mootnick 2006; Roos and Nadler 2005; Roos et al. 2007; Thinh et al. 2010, 2011).

Nomascus nasutus has been variously considered either as a species in its own right (sometimes as conspecific with N. hainanus), or as a subspecies of N. concolor; it is here recognized as a species distinct from N. hainanus and N. concolor, based on differences in vocalizations and fur colouration as well as genetic evidence (Mootnick and Fan 2011; Van Ngoc Thinh et al. 2010, 2011; Feng et al. 2014).
Arctocebus aureus was originally considered a subspecies of A. calabarensis but described as a full species by Maier (1980).
Until the late 1980s, this species was commonly treated as one of two subspecies of Arctocebus calabarensis, with the other being A. c. aureus; aureus is now treated as a full species.

This taxon was formerly considered a subspecies of Nycticebus coucang, but was elevated to species level by Roos (2003) and Chen et al. (2006). See also Nekaris and Jaffe (2007). The smallest of the Indonesian slow lorises (350 g-600 g), it is not only distinguished genetically from the others, but also by its pale golden to red fur, virtual lack of markings on its head, and consistent absence of a second upper incisor (Groves 1971, 1998; Ravosa 1998; Chen et al. 2006; Nekaris and Jaffe 2007). Nycticebus menagensis is very pale with a light contrasting facemask and round or diffuse-edged upper circumocular patch. Lower circumocular patch is variable and sometimes extends below the zygomatic arch, it has a narrow interocular stripe, crown patch is mostly diffused, the ears are usually naked, and the preauricular hair band is variable but mainly wide (Munds et al. 2013).

This taxon formerly included a number of subspecies that have subsequently been identified as unique species. A small hybridization zone is found between this species and Nycticebus bengalensis in southern peninsular Thailand. Further taxonomic revision may be necessary (Lim et al. 2007, K. A. Nekaris unpubl. data). Some authors consider the form from the Natuna islands to be a unique subspecies, N. c. natunae (Chasen 1935, Indrawan and Rangkuti 2001). Others consider the form from northern Sumatra to be a distinct taxon N. hilleri; we follow that here and exclude northern Sumatra from this assessment.Nekaris and Jaffe (2007) measured 16 N. coucang originating from Sumatra and reported the following average morphometric parameters for these individuals, which varied from those of N. hilleri: weight: 594 g; head length 62 mm; muzzle length 23.3 mm; head breath 45 mm; head body length 268 mm; hand span 54 mm; foot span 67 mm; ear length 17 mm (Nekaris and Jaffe 2007).

All Pithecia taxonomy follows Marsh (2014).

Kobayashi and Langguth (1994) first reported and later described (Kobayashi and Langguth 1999) Callicebus coimbrai after analyzing five specimens collected at three sites of the coastal Atlantic Forest in Sergipe State, in northeastern Brazil. Based on their study of this new species, along with previous craniometric studies by Kobayashi (1995), Kobayashi and Langguth (1999) argued that the titis of eastern Brazil constitute a separated group within the genus —  the personatus group — and should be considered a full species rather than a subspecies of C. personatus. In addition to C. coimbrai the authors listed C. nigrifrons, C. personatus, C. melanochir and C. barbarabrownae for that group. Based on molecular data, Byrne et al. (2016) proposed to split the genus Callicebus in three different genera (Callicebus, Cheracebus and Plecturocebus), with the ‘personatus group’ as the only component in the genus Callicebus.

This species was previously known as Callicebus modestus (Lönnberg, 1939). Taxonomical assessments of titi monkeys recognized different numbers of species groups (Hershkovitz 1963, 1988, 1990, Kobayashi 1995, Kobayashi and Langguth 1999, van Roosmalen et al. 2002, Groves 2005). A completely new phylogenetic arrangement of these primates (Byrne et al. 2016), divides Callicebus into three genera: Cheracebus, Callicebus, and Plecturocebus. According to this last assessment, Plecturocebus modestus is found in the donacophilus group, along with P. donacophilus, P. oenanthe, P. olallae, P. pallescens and P. urubambensis.The morphological similarity between P. modestus and P. olallae demanded further investigation (Tarifa 1996, Anderson 1997, Felton et al. 2006). Recent field observations (Martinez and Wallace 2007), as well as opportunistically collected specimens (Martinez et al. 2013), and results from a scat-based genetic study (Wallace et al. 2013, Barreta et al. 2019) support the taxonomic separation of P. modestus and P. olallae.

Byrne et al. (2016) have separated the genus Callicebus into three new genera, namely: Cheracebus (torquatus group sensu Roosmalen et al. (2002)), Plecturocebus (cupreus + moloch + donacophilus groups sensu Roosmalen et al. (2002)), and Callicebus (personatus group, sensu Roosmalen et al. (2002)). According to Byrne et al. (2016), Plecturocebus includes 22 species and P. dubius is a junior synonym of P. caligatus. However, the situation is still under debate, and we will regard these as two separate taxa until further evidence has been published.

Kobayashi and Langguth (1999) and van Roosmalen et al. (2002) recognize five species groups for Callicebus: cupreus, donacophilus, moloch, personatus and torquatus. Based on craniometric and other morphological studies, Kobayashi (1995) and Kobayashi and Langguth (1999) argued that C. nigrifrons – and the other forms of the personatus group should be considered full species rather than subspecies of C. personatus, as proposed by Hershkovitz (1988, 1990) and Groves (2001). In addition to C. nigrifrons they listed C. personatus, C. melanochir, C. barbarabrownae and C. coimbrai. Based on molecular data, Byrne et al. (2016) proposed to split Callicebus in three different genera (Callicebus, Cheracebus and Plecturocebus), with the species of the personatus group as the only components of the genus Callicebus in this new arrangement.

Kobayashi and Langguth (1999) and van Roosmalen et al. (2002) recognize five species groups – cupreus, donacophilus, moloch, personatus and torquatus. Callicebus brunneus belongs to the moloch group, which also includes: Callicebus baptista, Callicebus bernhardi, Callicebus cinerascens, Callicebus hoffmannsi and Callicebus moloch. Based on molecular data, Byrne et al. (2016) reassed the Callicebus genus and placed this species in the genus Plecturocebus. Ferrari et al. (2000) report the possible existence of a contact zone between P. brunneus and P. moloch in southern Rondonia, somewhere between the Serra dos Pacaás Novos, to the north, and the Chapada dos Parecis, to the south. The characteristics of this contact zone remain unclear, i.e. whether sympatry or even hybridization occurs, but it is interesting to note that at two sites located south of the Pacaás Novos, some monkeys observed were relatively lightly-coloured (more similar to P. moloch) in contrast with the typical dun tones of P. brunneus. Local residents also confirmed the existence of two distinct types of titis in different areas at this site.

(2002) and Callicebus (personatus-group, sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002).  According to Byrne et al. (2016), Plecturocebus includes 22 species.  Callicebus baptista’s Lönnberg, 1939, type locality is unknown. Restricted by P. Hershkovitz (1963) to the Lago do Baptista, in the Brazilian state of Amazonas.  It was considered to be a subspecies of C. hoffmannsi by P. Hershkovitz (1990). In 2001, Groves (2002) listed it as a full species. The species is monotypic (Mittermeir et al. 2013).

(2002) and Callicebus (personatus-group, sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002). According to Byrne et al. (2016), Plecturocebus includes 22 species.

Callicebus melanochir belongs to the personatus group, which also includes: Callicebus barbarabrownae, Callicebus coimbrai, Callicebus nigrifrons and Callicebus personatus. Following the taxonomic revision of Byrne et al. (2016), the genus Callicebus is now endemic to Brazil.

Hill (1960) listed three species of bearded saki: Chiropotes chiropotes, C. satanas and C. albinasa [sic]. Hershkovitz (1985) described a new species, utahickae, and classified satanas and utahickae as subspecies of C. chiropotes. Groves (2001, 2005) followed the taxonomy of Hershkovitz (1985). The three subspecies of Chiropotes satanas (satanas, chiropotes and utahicki) are here listed as full species following the recommendation of Silva-Júnior and Figueiredo (2002), Figueiredo et al. (2006), and Silva-Júnior et al.(2013). Bonvicino et al. (2003) resurrected the name Chiropotes israelita (Spix, 1823) for the bearded saki discovered by Boubli (2002) to the west of the Rio Branco, a tributary of the Rio Negro, Amazonas, Brazil. Genetic and pelage differences, notably a greenish brown (olive) dorsum as opposed to light golden brown as is typical of C. chiropotes, distinguish it from the bearded sakis of the Guianas to the east of the Rio Branco. There is however, a possible confusion concerning the correct names. Silva-Júnior and Figueiredo (2002) argued that the form west of the Rio Branco is, correctly Chiropotes chiropotes (Humboldt, 1811), according to its type locality, and the form to the east of the Rio Branco, extending through the states of Pará and Amapá, and into the Guianas (Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana) is C. sagulatus (Traill, 1821) from Demerara (see Silva-Júnior et al. (2013). Doubts still remain, however, concerning Hershkovitz’s interpretation of Humboldt’s type locality of C. chiropotes, which would accordingly alter the nomenclature (J. P. Boubli, pers. comm). With the further research and phylogenetic analysis, both Traill’s sagulatus and Spix’s israelita may be valid species names for different populations of this wide ranging genus.
