Until recently, Trachypithecus margarita was included in T. germaini. Genetic data (mtDNA studies) and phenotypical characters supports separate species status, though additional study will be needed for confirmation, since the study was based on a few samples from Cambodia and Viet Nam (including samples from animals of unknown origin) and no samples from Lao PDR (Roos et al., 2008). It is considered to be part of the cristatus group (T. cristatus, T. auratus, T. mauritus, T. germaini and T. selangorensis) (Hoang Minh Duc et al. 2012, Nadler and Brockman 2014, Nadler et al. 2005, Roos et al. 2008).

Before 2021, this species was thought to occur in the North Atlantic and in warm-temperate waters of the Southern Hemisphere, with a gap in its distribution in tropical waters; it was the only beaked whale species thought to have an anti-tropical distribution. The Southern Hemisphere population was recently described as a new species (Carroll et al. 2021), and M. mirus is now considered to be limited to the North Atlantic.

According to Gardner (2007) seven subspecies are recognized: Bradypus variegatus boliviensis (Gray, 1871); B.v. brasiliensis Blainville, 1840; B.v. ephippiger R.A. Philippi, 1870; B.v. gorgon O. Thomas, 1926; B.v. infuscatus Wagler, 1831; B.v. trivittatus Cornalia, 1849; and B.v. variegates Schinz, 1825. However, a revision of the taxonomic rearrangement of B. variegatus is needed (Silva et al. 2018). For instance, a recent mitochondrial DNA study proposed that the morphological subspecies B. variegatus boliviensis is invalid and Bolivian specimens belong to B. variegatus infuscatus (Ruiz-García et al. 2020).

Five subspecies are recognized by Gardner and Naples (2007). Molecular analysis (mitochondrial DNA) indicates a deep divergence between individuals from northern (Choloeps hoffmanni hoffmanni) and southern (C. h. juruanus and C. h. pallescens) populations. It also supports the differentiation of three analysed subspecies (Moraes-Barros and Arteaga 2015). Further research including representatives of all described subspecies is needed to establish whether there are taxonomic differences between the two disjunct populations.
Three subspecies are recognized by Gardner (2007).

Gardner (2005) recognizes four subspecies of T. mexicana (T. m. mexicana, T. m. opistholeuca, T. m. instabilis, and T. m. punensis). It is likely that further taxonomic work is needed for this species.
There are four subspecies of T. tetradactyla (Gardner 2007).
Bradypus pygmaeus has only recently been described by Anderson and Handley (2001) as a separate species.

Byrne et al. 2016 separated the genus Callicebus into three genera, namely:  Cheracebus n. gen. for the torquatus group of the Orinoco, Negro and upper Amazon basins; Callicebus Thomas, 1903 for the (personatus group) of the Atlantic Forest and Northeast Brazil; and Plecturocebus n. gen. for donacophilus and moloch groups in the Amazon basin and Chaco region.An in-depth study regarding the identity and range C. torquatus by Byrne et al. (2020) revealed, that C. torquatus (Hoffmannsegg, 1807) was a senior synonym of C. purinus (Thomas, 1927), and, following Byrne et al. (2020), Cheracebus includes five named species, C. torquatus, C. lugens, C. lucifer, C. regulus and C. medemi. Cheracebus populations south of the Río Napo between the ríos Nanay and Tigre in Peru (Heymann et al. 2002; Aquino et al. 2008) probably belong to a distinct sixth species, as yet undescribed.

The species was first described by Cabrera in 1904 using morphological characters. It was then synonymized with Myotis nattereri until recently, when the use of mitochondrial and nuclear markers supported its differentiation as a valid species (Ibáñez et al. 2006; Salicini et al. 2011, 2013) within the group of species that conform the ‘nattereri' species complex.

This assessed concept of Myotis nattereri excludes M. bombinus (southeastern Siberia, northeastern China, Korea, Japan), Myotis schaubi (Armenia and western Iran), M. escalerai, M. crypticus, M. zenatius, M. hoveli, M. tschuliensis, as well as the former Myotis sp. C. (subpopulation endemic to Corsica), which was described as Myotis nustrale sp. nov. Ruedi, Beuneux & Puechmaille (Puechmaille et al. 2023) in late 2023.It also excludes the recently described Myotis crypticus Ruedi, Ibáñez, Salicini, Juste & Puechmaille, 2019 (central and northern Spain, southern France, through Italy and possibly southwestern Austria and western Switzerland; Simmons and Cirranello 2022).

There is marked genetic differentiation between populations on central and eastern islands in the archipelago, indicating that they have evolved in relative isolation for a long time (Salgueiro et al. 2004).
Unidentified Pipistrellus bats found in the Azores have recently been proposed to belong to this species, but this awaits confirmation.

This species is considered to be endemic to Europe, from Ireland to the Urals (Spitzenberger et al. 2006). The Asian subpopulations have been identified as separate species, Plecotus ognevi and P. sacrimontis. Some Spanish subpopulations were described as subspecies P. auritus begognae (Juste et al. 2004). The North African subpopulations are recognised as different species (Plecotus christii, Plecotus gaisleri).
This is a revised taxonomic concept for Plecotus austriacus. The Asian subpopulations are considered as distinct species (P. ariel, P. kozlovi, P. turkmenicus and P. wardi).
Identified as a new species by genetic analyses, this species combines morphological features of both P. austriacus and P. auritus.

Here we refer to P. teneriffae as the population of the Canary Islands. Northwest African populations previously assigned to P. teneriffae are currently included in P. gaisleri, and Balkan populations are assigned to P. austriacus. The taxonomic status of the species was confirmed by Spitzenberger et al. (2006). There are no significant genetic differences between populations on the islands of the Canary Archipelago where this species is found (Juste et al. 2004).

The type specimens for Felis bieti are mounted skin and skull collected by Prince Henry d’Orleans (~1889) and kept at the National Museum of Natural History, Paris, France. The type locality is described as “Tatsienlu, Central Szechwan” by Milne-Edwards (1892), restricted by Pousargues (1898) to “environ de Tongolo et de Ta-tsien-Lou”, and verified to be Dong E Luo (=Tongolo) Village, Xinduqiao Township, Kangding (=Tatsienlu or Tatsienlou) County, Garzê Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan, China. Three subspecies were once proposed, but two were considered misidentifications, therefore, the Chinese Mountain Cat is currently considered monotypic.Felis bieti bieti Milne-Edwards, 1892, the nominate subspecies distributed in E Qinghai, NW Sichuan, and Gansu, (includes pallida Buchner, 1892, Kweito and S Tatung Mts, Kansu = Guide and Datongshan range, E Qinghai; and subpallida Jacobi, 1923, Songpan, NW Sichuan);F. b. vellerosa Pocock, 1943; type locality near Yulinfu (=Yulin) on the borders of Ordos (Inner Mongolia) and N Shaanxi; also named the Ordos Cat, but suggested by Haltenorth 1953 as F. silvestris, and by Groves 1980 as F. catus; andF. b. chutuchta Birula, 1917; no type locality, possibly around the Goizso area of the Gobi Desert in Inner Mongolia or NW Ningxia; also named the Gobi Cat, synonym with F. bieti by Allen (1938), Pocock (1943, 1951), but suggested by Haltenorth (1953) and Groves (1980) as F. silvestris.The taxonomy of the species in relation to other wildcat taxa has not reached a unanimous agreement, though molecular phylogeny and population genetics are revealing a much clearer evolutionary and systematic pattern. The Chinese Mountain Cat has traditionally been considered a species (F. bieti). However, Haltenorth (1953) and Corbet (1978) stated that, once more specimens became available, analysis would show the Chinese Mountain Cat to be a subspecies of Felis silvestris. Driscoll et al. (2007) provided genetic evidence to indicate F. bieti to be a subspecies of F. silvestris, whilst Kitchener et al. (2009, 2017) attributed its species status again, based on morphological distinction and its potential sympatry with the Asiatic wildcat (F. s. ornata). Most recently, Yu et al. (2021) conducted a genome-wide analysis to render support of the Chinese Mountain Cat as equidistant with the Asiatic wildcat, and hence should be recognized as a wildcat subspecies, F. s. bieti. This study was based on whole genome sequencing and uniparentally inherited mitochondrial genome and Y-chromosome haplotypes of the Chinese Mountain Cat, Asiatic wildcat, and domestic cats, together with publicly available partial genomic data.Yu et al. (2021) calculated the coalescence time of F. s. catus, F. s. bieti, and F. s. ornata at around 1.5 million years ago during the Middle Pleistocene, results consistent with estimations from Li et al. (2016) and Johnson et al. (2006). Given the relatively deep divergence of the wildcat taxa, Yu et al. (2021) also proposed an alternative approach to resolve the conflict between the genomic pattern and current taxonomic nomenclature, which is to elevate all wildcat lineages, including the Asiatic wildcat (F. s. ornata) and African wildcat (F. s. lybica), to independent species, or F. ornata and F. lybica, respectively, thus retaining the Chinese Mountain Cat as F. bieti to be consistent. This proposition would however require a comprehensive analysis of whole genome data from all wildcat taxa, especially those from F. s. silvestris and F. s. lybica.The IUCN SSC Cat SG follows the revised taxonomy of Kitchener et al. (2017) until there is an update of this revision. Therefore, the Chinese Mountain Cat is currently treated as a separate species and assessed as such.

Six subspecies have been described (Ansell 1972; summarized in Cassinello 1998). However, apart from the fact that the morphological differences between them are not well defined, and there are several apparent zones of hybridization, relying exclusively on morphological traits is an obsolete and inadequate criterion to define subspecies. Therefore, and in order to re-evaluate aoudad subspecies distinction, a comprehensive genetic analysis of individuals from all the distinctive populations should be carried out. This would allow to properly identify genetic units that help redefining subspecific criteria and eventually allow undertaking proper conservation actions to protect the species (Cassinello 2015).

While taxonomy of serow has been confusing, this assessment follows Mori et al. 2019, which recognises C. rubidus as a full species of Capricornis. The Red Serow (as C .s. rubidus) was listed as Endangered (A2cd) in the 1996 IUCN Red List of Threatened Animals (IUCN 1996). However, this assessment probably included the red form of Himalayan Serow which was often attributed to this species, but it is currently included in C. sumatraensis (Duckworth and Zaw 2008).

authority: Tu, Csorba, Göorföl, Arai, Son, Thanh & Hasanin, 2015
taxonomicNotes: Earlier, trident bats found in karst areas between northeastern Viet Nam and Guangxi, China were referred to A. stoliczkanus, but are now considered as representatives of the recently described A. dongbacanus (Tu et al. 2015). Its original specific name, Aselliscus dongbacana, has been changed for gender agreement (Monadjem et al. 2019).

Genetic (Rosel et al. 1995) and morphological (Brownell et al. 1987) data suggest that Vaquitas are most closely related to porpoises in South America. Genetic data suggest divergence from two sister taxa (Burmeister’s Porpoise, Phocoena spinipinnis and Spectacled Porpoise Australophocaena dioptrica) in the Pleistocene (i.e., at least 2.5 million years ago).

This species originally was described as a subspecies of Megaerops wetmorei (Taylor 1934) by Francis (1989) and most literature reports from Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei list it under that name. However, Almeida et al. (2020) show that true wetmorei from the Philippines is morphologically distinct from albicollis. Genetically it is distinct from other Megaerops and instead appears to belong in the genus Ptenochirus. The separation of these species is supported by DNA barcode data that confirm M. albicollis is distinct from P. wetmorei and is more closely related to other species in the genus Megaerops (C. M. Francis, unpublished analyses of data from BoLD).

The intraspecific taxonomy of the Tiger (Panthera tigris) has been recently debated due to inconsistent results from various methodologies (Luo et al. 2004, Wilting et al. 2015, Kitchener et al. 2017, Liu et al. 2018). Luo et al. (2004) identify six subspecies on the analysis of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) while Wilting et al. (2015) classified Tigers into two subspecies based on data sets of several traits [morphological (craniodental and pelage), ecological, molecular]. These inconsistencies were partly attributed to the lack of genetic samples across the Tiger range. However, Liu et al. (2018) used whole-genome sequencing analyses from 32 voucher specimens that resolve six statistically robust monophyletic clades. The higher resolution of data obtained from nuclear genomes highlights little admixture and gene flow between the six subspecies. Nevertheless, there is incomplete congruence between mitochondrial and nuclear DNA results for P. t. amoyensis, suggesting the inclusion of more samples in future analysis to confirm its relationship with P. t. jacksoni.Liu et al. (2018) concluded that six extant subspecies exist based on genome-wide analysis:Amur Tiger (P. t. altaica): Russian Far East and northeastern China.Northern Indochinese Tiger (P. t. corbetti): Indochina north of the Malayan Peninsula.Malayan Tiger (P. t. jacksoni): Peninsular Malaysia.Sumatran Tiger (P. t. sumatrae): Sumatra.Bengal Tiger (P. t. tigris): Indian sub-continent.South China Tiger (P. t. amoyensis), although this subspecies has not been directly observed in the wild since the 1970s and is possibly extinct.Three subspecies previously recognised based on morphology are extinct:Bali Tiger (P. t. balica Schwarz, 1912): Bali. Javan Tiger (P. t. sondaica (Temminck, 1844)): Java.Caspian Tiger (P. t. virgata (Illiger, 1815)): dry river valleys of the Takla Makan, western slopes of the Tianshan mountains, Amudarya and Syrdarya river valleys, shores of the Caspian Sea, Elburz mountains, eastern Turkey, Tigris and Euphrates River valleys.However, given the varied interpretations of existing data, the taxonomy of this species is currently under review by the IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group.
Microcebus berthae is the name given to the diminutive Rufous-colored Mouse Lemur from Kirindy/CFPF, originally called M. myoxinus by Schmid and Kappeler (1994).

Presbytis femoralis formerly was regarded as a subspecies of P. melalophos (Thorington and Groves 1970, Medway 1983, Napier 1985, Oates et al. 1994), but later was recognized as a species with three subspecies: P. f. femoralis, P. f. percura and P. f. robinsoni (Groves 2001, Meyer et al. 2011, Groves and Roos 2013, Roos et al. 2014).Genetic data suggested that at least P. f. femoralis and P. f. robinsoni were different species (Ang 2010, Nijman 2019), which also agreed with their morphological characters. However, resolving all subspecies-level boundaries within banded langurs required data for P. f. percura, which was the least studied and only found in the Riau Province in Sumatra (Rizaldi et al. 2019). Complete mitochondrial genomes were later obtained for P. f. percura in the wild, and based on multiple species delimitation algorithms (PTP, ABGD, Objective Clustering) applied to a dataset covering 40 species and 43 subspecies of Asian colobines, all three subspecies of banded langurs were resurrected to species (Ang et al. 2020).Presbytis femoralis was described by Martin (1838) based on specimens collected by Raffles (1821) from Singapore. However, Martin (1838) gave the distribution as "Sumatra etc.", not mentioning Singapore explicitly, resulting in some confusion over the actual type locality (Miller 1934, Low and Lim 2015). Miller (1934) determined Singapore as the actual type locality, and the secretariat of the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature confirmed the authorship of P. femoralis as Martin, the year of publication as 1838, and the type locality as Singapore (Low and Lim 2015).Presbytis femoralis is uniform black on the dorsum with a white band traversing down the chest and abdomen, the inside of the humeri from the axilla, and the inside of the thighs (Raffles 1821, Martin 1838, Groves 2001). In contrast to the adult pelage, infants are born with a white coat with a broad black band from the head, along the spine, to the tail, and intersected by a black band passing along the shoulders to the outer surfaces of both forearms, forming a distinctive cruciform (cross-like) black pattern on the dorsum. A faint black line runs from the dark spinal stripe along the hind legs to the feet. The crown and facial hair are completely white from the frontal view. The forehead is slightly dark compared to the pale colour of the face (Pocock 1928, Ang et al. 2010).

The use of Lutra for four New World otter species (L. felina, L. canadensis, L. longicaudis, L. provocax) has been widespread in the past. Van Zyll de Jong (1972, 1987) separated this group into the genus Lontra based on morphological criteria, which was confirmed by Wozencraft (1993). Koepfli and Wayne (1998) and Koepfli et al. (2008) re-confirmed this classification based on molecular data. Thus, nowadays the generic name Lontra should be accepted as valid for all New World otters (except Pteronura).
Rhinopithecus brelichi was formerly considered a subspecies of Rhinopithecus roxellana, but is now accepted as specifically distinct (Groves 2001).

A second species of Hypogeomys is known from the subfossil record. Hypogeomys australis was still extant 4,400 years ago, and once occurred from southeastern Madagascar north to at least the Antsirabe region (Goodman and Rakotondravony 1996).

authority: Simmons, Flanders, Fils, Parker, Suter, Bamba, Douno, Keita, Morales, & Frick, 2021
taxonomicNotes: Species first described in 2021 after two individuals were caught in the Nimba Mountains in January 2018 as part of a biodiversity assessment. While Myotis nimbaensis shares similar features with three other large Myotis (subgenus Chrysopteron) species with orange dorsal fur occur in Africa (M. tricolor, M. welwitschii, and M. morrisi), it is easily distinguishable due to its body size and various color patterns (Simmons et al. 2021).
Recent taxonomic review has elevated this species from its former status as a subspecies of Antechinus swainsonii.

The taxonomic treatment of Petauroides volans is contested and not fully resolved. A single species has long been accepted. However, Jackson (2015) and Jackson and Groves (2015) recognised three species: Petauroides volans, P. minor and P. armillatus, based on limited published evidence. A subsequent genetic study provided some support to this treatment (McGregor et al. 2020), and the three species are currently listed in the American Society of Mammalogists Mammal Diversity Database (version 1.13). In its most recent conservation assessment, the Australian government recognised two species: P. volans (including P. armillatus) and P. minor (Threatened Species Scientific Committee 2022a,b). However, that split is not recognised in a recent taxonomic review of Australasian marsupials (Baker et al. 2023), by the Australasian Mammal Taxonomy Consortium (as at August 2024) and, following this, by Jackson (2023). The previous Red List account was for the single species, P. volans; until the taxonomy is fully resolved, and the IUCN SSC Australasian Marsupial and Monotreme Specialist Group continues to follow this treatment.
Spalax antiquus and S. istricus were previously considered to be synonyms of S. graecus, however they are now recognised as separate species.

Spalax istricus was previously listed as a subspecies of S. graecus but has since been recognized as a separate species due to recent molecular genetic and detailed morphological studies (Németh et al. 2013).The three known subpopulations, separated by the Carpathian Mountains, can be regarded as separate species, and assigned to already described taxa, this includes the Oltenia Blind Mole-rat.

Hill (1953) listed six subspecies of L. tardigradus. Groves (1989) recognized a single species of L. tardigradus with three “sharply distinct” subspecies in Sri Lanka and two in India (see Schulze and Meier 1995). In 1998, however, Groves argued for two species: the very small and narrow snouted monotypic red form (L. tardigradus) from the wet zone of Sri Lanka, and the larger grey or ashy form (L. lydekkerianus) in India (L. l. lydekkerianus and L. l. malabaricus) and Sri Lanka (L. l. grandis and L. l. nycticeboides). This taxonomy was followed in Groves (2001, 2005) and Brandon-Jones et al. (2004).A phylogenetic analysis by Pozzi et al. (2015) and a morphological study by Gamage et al. (2017) also confirmed the validity of the two species. In 2004, Nekaris and Jaywardene showed that nycticeboides, also from the wet zone of Sri Lanka, is a subspecies of tardigradus, contra Groves (2001, 2005) and Brandon-Jones et al. (2004), who placed it as a subspecies of lydekkerianus. Groves (2001) was of the opinion that museum specimens of nordicus Hill, 1933, were indistinguishable from those of L. l. grandis and considered this form, therefore, to be a junior synonym (see Brandon-Jones et al. 2004). Nekaris and Bearder (2006), Nekaris (2003, 2013) and Gamage et al. (2017), however, argued for the validity of nordicus as a subspecies of L. lydekkerianus. Gamage et al. (2017) argued for the existence of a fifth subspecies in south-east Sri Lanka that was previously believed to be L. l. nordicus–L. l. uva, which they indicated may even be a distinct species. In 2017, therefore, L. lydekkerianus was believed to comprise five subspecies: L. l. lydekkerianus and L. l. malabaricus in India, and L. l. grandis, L. l. nycticeboides and L. l. uva in Sri Lanka. Gamage et al. (2019) subsequently carried out a phylogenetic analysis, which they believed largely confirmed their arrangement for the Sri Lankan forms.

Until relatively recently, this species was classified as a subspecies of Macaca nemestrina. There is some hybridization with M. nemestrina in a small area of southern peninsular Thailand, and on the  islands of Phuket and Yao Yai (Groves 2001).Assigned to the nemestrina species group including M. nemestrina, M. leonina, M. silenus, M. pagensis. Restricted hybridization with M. nemestrina where their ranges are contiguous in peninsular Thailand. (Between 8° and 9°N) at the southern end of Isthmus of Kra.

Until recently, the silvered langurs of Indochina were considered conspecific with the Sundaic Silvered Langur (Trachypithecus cristatus), which was thought to be widely distributed across parts on Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Viet Nam, Cambodia, Lao PDR, and Myanmar. During the past few years, genetic analyses have supported the assignment of all non-Sundaic populations to the species T. germaini, and subsequently called for a further division of the Indochinese taxon into two species (Groves 2001, Nadler et al. 2005, Roos et al. 2008). The Indochinese populations occurring west of the Mekong River in Viet Nam, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Thailand, and Myanmar have been  attributed to T. germaini, or the Indochinese Silvered Langur, while populations occurring east of the Mekong River in Viet Nam, Cambodia, and Lao PDR have been attributed to T. margarita, or the Annamese Silvered Langur (Hoang Minh Duc et al. 2012a, Nadler and Brockman 2014, Nadler et al. 2005, Roos et al. 2008, Roos et al. 2014). Recent data based on a study of populations separated by the Mekong River provide support for the species split but indicate that the Mekong, while limiting gene flow, is not an impermeable barrier (Moody 2018). Furthermore, this analysis revealed that a population in north-eastern Cambodia was distinguishable compared to other study populations, both west and east of the Mekong. This may be indicative of a species barrier farther east of the Mekong that extends into Viet Nam but additional sampling of populations in both Lao and Viet Nam are critical to better understanding the limits between these species (Moody 2018). Thus, taxonomic analyses should be expanded outside of Cambodia with the aim of clarifying the boundary between these taxa and the limits of their distribution.

Byrne et al. 2016 have separated the genus Callicebus into three new genera, namely:  Cheracebus (Torquatus group sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002), Plecturocebus (Cupreus + moloch groups sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002 and Callicebus (personatus group, sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002).  According to Byrne et al. (2016), Cheracebus includes six species, C. torquatus, C. lugens, C. lucifer, C. purinus, C. regulus and C. medemi.

Byrne et al. (2016) have separated the genus Callicebus into three new genera, namely:  Cheracebus (Torquatus group sensu Van Roosmalen et al 2002), Plecturocebus (Cupreus + moloch groups sensu Van Roosmalen et al. 2002) and Callicebus (personatus group, sensu Van Roosmalen et al. 2002).  According to Byrne et al. (2016) , Cheracebus includes six species, C. torquatus, C. lugens, C. lucifer, C. purinus, C. regulus and C. medemi. Simia lugens Humboldt, 1811, vicinity of San Fernando de Atabapo, at the confluence of the ríos Orinoco and Guaviare, Amazonas, Venezuela.

Byrne et al. 2016 have separated the genus Callicebus into three new genera, namely:  Cheracebus (Torquatus group sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002), Plecturocebus (Cupreus + moloch groups sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002 and Callicebus (personatus group, sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002). According to Byrne et al. (2016), Cheracebus includes six species, C. torquatus, C. lugens, C. lucifer, C. purinus, C. regulus and C. medemi.

Byrne et al. 2016 have separated the genus Callicebus into three new genera, namely:  Cheracebus (Torquatus group sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002), Plecturocebus (Cupreus + moloch groups sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002 and Callicebus (personatus group, sensu Roosmalen et al. 2002).  According to Byrne et al. (2016), Cheracebus includes six species, C. torquatus, C. lugens, C. lucifer, C. purinus, C. regulus and C. medemi.

Hill (1953) listed six subspecies of Loris tardigradus. Groves (1989) recognized a single species, L. tardigradus, with three “sharply distinct” subspecies in Sri Lanka and two in India (see Schulze and Meier 1995). In 1998, however, Groves argued for two species: the very small and narrow snouted monotypic red form (L. tardigradus) from the wet zone of Sri Lanka, and the larger grey or ashy form (L. lydekkerianus) in India (two subspecies) and Sri Lanka (two subspecies). This taxonomy was followed in Groves (2001, 2005) and Brandon-Jones et al. (2004).A phylogenetic analysis by Pozzi et al. (2015) and a morphological study by Gamage et al. (2017) also confirmed the validity of the two species. In 2004, Nekaris and Jaywardene showed that nycticeboides, also from the wet zone of Sri Lanka, is a subspecies of tardigradus, contra Groves (2001, 2005) and Brandon-Jones et al. (2004), who placed it as a subspecies of lydekkerianus. Gamage et al. (2017) argued that the slender loris from Mirigama, Gampaha District, Western Province of Sri Lanka was unique in its facial features, and cranial and post-cranial morphology, and distinct as such from L. t. tardigradus south of its range. They named it L. t. parvus. They also found evidence for a distinct, high-altitude (above 800 m) taxon in the southwestern wet zone in the Deniyaya-Rakwana mountains, which they declined to name pending more information. As such in 2017, L. tardigradus was believed to comprise three subspecies: L. t. tardigradus, L. t. nycticeboides, and L. t. parvus all from Sri Lanka. This is the taxonomy that is followed by the Primate Specialist Group.Gamage et al. (2019) subsequently carried out a phylogenetic analysis, which they believed largely confirmed this arrangement for the Sri Lankan lorises, but this was shown to be insufficient by Nijman et al. (2020). As such, more robust genetic studies are needed.

Lepus castroviejoi was described relatively recently, being separated from L. granatensis, a split supported by genetic evidence. While the range of L. castroviejoi partially overlaps that of L. granatensis and L. europaeus on the Iberian Peninsula, no hybridization has been detected with these forms. Recent studies have shown that instead, based on ecological, molecular and morphological characteristics, it is most closely related to L. corsicanus; some believe these two are conspecific (Alves et al. 2008, Acevedo et al. 2014, Ballesteros 2018). Additionally, two different occurrences of introgression of mtDNA from L. timidus into L. castroviejoi have been documented – indicating that these two forms have come into contact and hybridized two different times in the past, most recently during the last deglaciation (Melo-Ferreira et al. 2005, 2012; Ballesteros 2018). No subspecies or geographic variation in L. castroviejoi have been described (Flux and Angermann 1990, Hoffmann and Smith 2005, Ballesteros 2018).

The Iberian Hare was historically classified as a variety of the Cape Hare, Lepus capensis, under subspecies L. c. granatensis (Chapman and Flux 1990), but morphological analyses confirmed the validity of the specific status of the Iberian Hare, and the distinction from the Cape Hare (Palacios 1983). When compared to the other hare species inhabiting the Iberian Peninsula, the interspecific morphological differences also allow their distinction (Palacios 1983).

Twelve subspecies were recognised by Hung and Law (2016):Lutra lutra angustifrons in North Africa;Lutra lutra aurobrunnea in Garhwal Himalayas in northern India and higher altitudes in Nepal;Lutra lutra barang in southeast Asia (Thailand, Viet Nam, Indonesia and Sumatra);Lutra lutra chinensis in southern China and Taiwan;Lutra lutra hainana in Hainan Island, China;Lutra lutra kutab in northern India (Kashmir);Lutra lutra lutra is the most widely distributed, spanning from Portugal to South Korea;Lutra lutra meridionalis in from Georgia through Armenia, Azerbaijan and IranLutra lutra monticola in northern India (Punjab, Kumaon, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim and Assam) Nepal, Bhutan and Myanmar;Lutra lutra nair in southern India and Sri Lanka;Lutra lutra seistanica in Afghanistan, Eastern Iran, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan; The extinct Japanese subspecies, Lutra lutra whiteleyi, was considered a distinct species (L. nippon) by Suzuki et al. (1996).

Nyctophilus holtorum was described recently as a new species (Parnaby et al. 2021). It was excised from N. gouldi sensu stricto, which is distributed broadly around the eastern and southern margin of Australia, from Cairns in Queensland to the Nullarbor Plain in South Australia. It is a geographic isolate, occurring in the mesic forests and woodlands of the south-west of Western Australia. Genetic markers demonstrated that N. holtorum is more closely related to N. daedalus (based on one sample from the Pilbara region of north-western Australia) than to N. gouldi in eastern and southern Australia.For the purpose of identification, N. holtorum is diagnosable based on mitochondrial DNA sequence divergence (COI gene) of ca 5% from N. gouldi, and ca 12.1% from sympatric N. geoffroyi (no samples were available from sympatric N. major); plus combinations of subtle skull and snout characters and body size (Parnaby 2010, Parnaby et al. 2021). Several key morphological features allow the three sympatric long-eared bat species in the south-west of Western Australia to be differentiated from one another. Its forearm length of 38–44 mm (Parnaby et al. 2021), and the posterior portion of the noseleaf has a simple, straight groove (muzzle Type 2 of Churchill 2008; see Figure 5 of Parnaby et al. 2021). By contrast, N. geoffroyi has a smaller body size (forearm less than c. 42 mm; Churchill 2008), and the posterior portion of its noseleaf has a Y-shaped groove (muzzle Type 1 in Churchill 2008); and N. major has a larger body size (forearm 42–49 mm; Parnaby 2010) and lacks a groove in the posterior portion of the noseleaf (muzzle Type 4 in Churchill 2008). Other diagnostic features of the skull and baculum (Parnaby 2010, Parnaby et al. 2021) are not readily observed in live specimens. Echolocation calls of the three sympatric Nyctophilus cannot be distinguished reliably (Pennay et al. 2004, Webala et al. 2011).

Nyctophilus gouldi has recently been revised and is now considered to be restricted to eastern Australia. Animals from far southwest Western Australia previously attributed to N. gouldi are now considered to belong to the species Nyctophilus holtorum (Parnaby et al. 2021).

A taxonomic study published by Irwin (2017) resolved the taxonomic status of four similar-sized Nyctimene that occur on the island of New Guinea and provided revised diagnoses for three of them. The description and diagnosis of this new species was provided, along with information on distribution based on examinations of specimens.
Well established, distinct monotypic species (Kitchener et al. 2017).

The taxonomy of the genus has been debated, but recent work supports the use of the name Lontra rather than Lutra for New World river otters (van Zyll de Jong 1982, Larivière and Walton 1998, Wozencraft 1993, Koepfli and Wayne 1998). Three proposed subspecies are suggested by their present disjunct distribution: L. longicaudis annectens, restricted to México, Central America and north-western South America; L. l. enudris, distributed across the Amazon region, from eastern Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru to north-western Bolivia and northern Brazil; and L. l. longicaudis, southern part of its distribution in South America (Larivière 1999, Trinca et al. 2012, Hernández-Romero et al. 2018).

Three regional subspecies originally described by Wilson et al. (1991) have been confirmed by Cronin et al. (1996): Enhydra lutris lutris (Linnaeus, 1758) from Japan in the southwest Pacific throughout the Asian range of the Kuril Islands to the Kamchatka Peninsula and the Commander Islands, E. l. kenyoni from the western Aleutian Islands to Prince William Sound, Alaska, USA, along the Pacific coast of Canada and into Oregon state in the continental USA, and E. l. nereis (Merriam, 1904) from central to southern California, USA.

Linnaeus' amphibius and terrestris, both proposed in 1758 on the same page, are now considered conspecific by most researchers. As shown by Corbet (1978), amphibius has a priority over terrestris, based on Blasius (1857) as the first reviser. At one point, this species was split into A. amphibius and A. scherman (Panteleyev 2001). Arvicola amphibius is larger, with shaggy pelage and ortodont incisors, and is associated with aquatic environments; A. scherman is smaller, with softer pelage, more reduced plantar and palmar tubercles, and the upper incisors strongly projecting forwards and has fossorial habits (Panteleyev 2001).However, the taxonomy of the A. amphibius group is more complex. Considering genetic distances and other biological data, it is suggested that the Italian lineage corresponds to a separate species (Arvicola italicus; Castiglia et al. 2016). The three other lineages correspond to phylogeographic variations of a single species (A. amphibius), encompassing the former A. amphibius, Arvicola terrestris, Arvicola scherman, and Arvicola monticola (Chevret et al. 2020, Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).
Talpa aquitania was recently recognised as a distinct species, separated from T. europaea, based on mtDNA analyses (Nicolas et al. 2017).

Specimens of Talpa martinorum were previously classified as T. caeca or as T. levantis. Following molecular analysis, T martinorum was recognised as a distinct species in 2018 (Kryštufek et al. 2018).
Specimens from Sulawesi assigned to the previously recognized Pteropus arquatus and P. argentatus are now recognized as Acerodon celebensis (Musser et al. 1982, Flannery 1995).

The taxonomy of all the canids, including Lycaon pictus, is currently under review by the Canid Specialist Group. Standard taxonomic texts recognise five subspecies: L. pictus pictus in southern Africa, L. pictus lupinus in eastern Africa, L. pictus somalicus in north-eastern Africa Africa, L. pictus sharicus in central Africa, and L. pictus manguensis in West Africa (Wilson and Reeder 2005). Morphological and genetic data from southern and eastern Africa initially tended to support the pictus/lupinus division (Girman et al. 1993); however, later analyses suggested greater mixing between the two regions (Girman et al. 2001). Ongoing genomic analyses over a broader geographical area (Ramage et al. in prep) will inform the Canid Specialist Group assessment.
The species was considered to consist of two allopatric chromosomal races (“arvalis” and “obscurus”: Wilson and Reeder 2005) but these are now treated as two distinct species (Tourgard et al. 2013).

It has been argued, on the basis of mandibular measurements, that Crocidura canariensis should be treated as a subspecies of C. sicula (Sarà 1996). However, other morphological, ecological, palaeontological and molecular evidence supports specific status (Michaux et al. 1991, Hutterer et al. 1992). Genetic distances suggest that C. canariensis and C. sicula diverged approximately five million years ago (Vogel et al. 2003), and both share karyotype with C. tarfayaensis (Vogel et al. 2006).
Microtus agrestis no longer includes M. rozianus nor M. lavernedii, which are considered distinct species (see Paupério et al. 2012 and Kryštufek 2017).

Microtus liechtensteini is part of the Microtus multiplex species-complex. Its formerly continuous range in the Alps was split into three parts during the last glaciation which led to the evolution of three species: Microtus liechtensteini (south of the Alps east of the river Adige and Balkan mountains), Microtus multiplex (south of the Alps west of the river Adige), and M. bavaricus (north of the Alps in a small refuge in Bavaria and the northern Tyrol) (Haring et al. 2000, Spitzenberger et al. 2000, Spitzenberger 2002, Musser and Carleton 2005).However, Martínková et al. (2007) found little molecular divergence between Microtus liechtensteini and M. bavacicus, and the latter is placed as a synonym of Microtus liechtensteini by the Mammal Diversity Database (ASM 2023), and this assessment follows that placement.

Following genetic sequencing studies, it is recognised that Microtus guentheri excludes M. hartingi (found in Anatolia and the Balkans) (Kryštufek et al. 2009) and M. mustersi (North Africa) (Thanou et al. 2020).
Microtus hyperboreus was considered to be a separate species, but most recent genetic and morphometric studies demonstrate that it is conspecific with Alexandromys middendorfii (Burgin et al. 2020).

This species is now recognised as distinct from Sciurus meridionalis which was previously described as a subspecies of S. vulgaris. S. meridionalis is now considered a separate species based on morphological and genetic data and is restricted to Calabria (southwestern Italy).
Formerly considered as a subspecies of Sicista subtilis, but now recognized as a separate species based on karyotype and DNA data (Kovalskaya et al. 2011, Lebedev et al. 2020).

authority: Cserkész, Fülöp, Almerekova, Kondor, Laczkó & Sramkó, 2019
taxonomicNotes: Significant genetic differences noted by Cserkész et al. (2019) lead to the description of the Zhetysu Alatau population of Sicista tianshanica as a new species: S. zhetysuica.

The suaveolens species group is extremely complex and includes several cryptic species and forms of intermediate status. Currently, Crocidura suaveolens in its broad sense has been split into three species: C. shantungensis (eastern Asia), C. gueldenstaedtii (majority of European range and southwestern Asia) and C. suaveolens proper (Bannikova et al. 2006, Burgin et al. 2020). This species is further divided into 3 subspecies: C. s. suaveolens (European range as far east as the Ural Mts.), C. s. iliensis Miller 1901 (Asiatic part of the range except Pamir Mts.), and C. s. pamirensis Ognev 1928 (Pamir Mts.) (Zaytsev et al. 2014); subspecific classification of shrews in Mongolia and China not resolved. Crocidura suaveolens includes here C. gmelini, following the Mammal Diversity Database (ASM 2022).

Previously, Crocidura gueldenstaedtii was classified as C. suaveolens. Genetic sequencing has recently supported the splitting of C. gueldenstaedtii from C. suaveolens and revised status as a distinct species (see Bannikova et al. 2006, İbiş et al. 2022). Crocidura gueldenstaedtii, however, remains part of the complex (or superspecies) C. suaveolens group which contains several close species and semi-species.

Neomys anomalus was described from Spain by Cabrera (1907) and originally included N. milleri with a range thought to extend across much of mainland Europe (see Querejeta and Castresana 2018). Studies have since confirmed the genetic differentiation between N. anomalus and N. milleri (Castiglia et al. 2007, Igea et al. 2015); both are now considered distinct species, with N. anomalus distributed in the Iberian Peninusla, and N. milleri distributed from northeastern Spain through Europe to Russia.
Neomys milleri was previously regarded as a subspecies of Neomys anomalus, but officially elevated to species status in 2015 following DNA analysis (Igea et al. 2015).

It was formally considered the Valais chromosome race of the Common Shrew Sorex araneus (2n = 24/25, FN = 40). Brünner et al. (2002) argued that morphological, karyotypic, and genetic differences warranted recognition as a distinct species. S. antinorii likely diverged from the other taxa of the S. araneus group during the late Pleistocene glaciation (see Yannic et al. 2012). It should also be noted that S. arunchi is now included in S. antinorii based on recent genetic analyses.

Molecular analysis supports species status for two allopatric lineages of the Caucasian mole, with Talpa caucasica recognised as the northern lineage found in the North Caucasus, and a southern lineage represented by Talpa ognevi from Georgia and Türkiye (Bannikova et al. 2015). It is estimated that the split of the two species dates back to the second half of the Pliocene (2.5-Myr) (Bannikova et al. 2015).

Molecular analysis supports species status for two allopatric lineages of the Caucasian mole, with Talpa caucasica recognised as the northern lineage found in the North Caucasus, and a southern lineage represented by Talpa ognevi from Georgia and Türkiye (Bannikova et al. 2015). It is estimated that the split of the two species dates back to the second half of the Pliocene (2.5-Myr) (Bannikova et al. 2015).
This species was previously included within Talpa levantis, but genetic evidence supports its elevation to species status (Bannikova et al. 2015), as reviewed in Kryštufek and Motokawa (2018).

Molecular evidence suggests that Talpa levantis contains two allopatric cryptic species of western and eastern lineages, but the nomenclature is unresolved (Bannikova et al. 2015, Demırtaş et al. 2020). This species previously included T. martinorum and T. talyschensis which are both now recognised as distinct species (Kryštufek et al. 2018).

authority: Cucchi, Orth, Auffray, Renaud, Fabre, Catalan, Hadjisterkotis, Bonhomme & Vigne, 2006
taxonomicNotes: This species was described by Cucchi et al. (2006): "A new species of the genus Mus has been discovered on the island of Cyprus, namely Mus cypriacus. Molecular phylogeny of complete D-loop sequences, as well as that of a nuclear gene intron (ABP), evidence that this new taxa is not an island variant but deserves a species rank on its own, as a sister species of Mus macedonicus and Mus spicilegus, the two closest mainland relatives. Classical and geometric morphometry provide diagnostic morphological criteria separating Mus cypriacus from European species."Genetic and archaeological evidence suggest that the common ancestor of M. cypriacus and M. macedonicus arrived on Cyprus during the Middle Pleistocene by a founder event on a natural raft (Cucchi et al. 2006). This species is one of only three surviving endemic mammal species on Mediterranean islands that originate from ancient natural colonization events (Gippoliti and Amori 2006).

Its phylogenetic position was studied by Jaarola et al. (2004). It is the sole extant representative of the subgenus Iberomys which has been suggested to be a seperate genus from Microtus (Cuenca-Bescós et al. 2014).

Sometimes considered as a subspecies of Microtus duodecimcostatus, but its specific status has been reconfirmed by analysis of karyotype, molecular genetics and molar pattern (Kryštufek 1999, Jaarola et al. 2004). A chromosomally polymorphic species; relationships are unknown (Wilson and Reeder 2005). It should be noted that two Greek regions, Evvoia Island and Attica Pref., hold isolated vole populations which were originally considered part of the M. thomasi distribution. Because of their genetic, karyological and morphological differentiation; they were grouped into a distinct subspecies, namely M. thomasi atticus. Laboratory crosses among wild caught “atticus” and “thomasi” individuals failed to produce viable and fertile hybrids. This is strong evidence suggesting that there are two sister-species, M. thomasi and M. atticus. M. atticus would represent a Greek endemic and a new mammal species for Europe but has not been formally described yet.
A. mystacinus has been split into two separate species: A. mystacinus and A. epimelas (Wilson and Reeder 2005).

Molecular data suggest that this taxon might in fact consist of two species, although further research is required to confirm this (Kryštufek et al. 2007). Genetic data clearly indicate that the Balkan Snow Vole is composed of three historically isolated, independently evolving sets of subpopulations that can be regarded as evolutionarily significant units (ESUs).
Eastern populations are now considered as a separate species, M. liechtensteini (Wilson and Reeder 2005).
Some authors consider Microtus pyrenaicus a synonym of Microtus gerbei, although there is debate about which name is appropriate (Musser and Carleton 2005).
Formerly considered a subspecies of Microtus savii, but now regarded as a separate species (Wilson and Reeder 2005).

Originally considered as a subspecies of M. savii, this species was elevated to species based on differences in sex chromosomes (Galleni et al. 1994) and by genetic and morphological-morphometric data (Bezerra et al. 2016).

For a long time, the westernmost representatives of the genus Spalax were identified as a single species, Spalax graecus. According to the recent studies (Németh et al. 2013, Csorba et al. 2015) the three known subpopulations, separated by the Carpathian Mountains, represent separate species which can be assigned to described taxa. One of them is Spalax antiquus Méhely’s Blind Mole-rat. The separation of Méhely’s Blind Mole-rat as a distinct species is highly supported by the combined evidences of morphology, multilocus phylogeny, biogeographical evidences and species congruence with past tectonic and climatic events (Németh et al. 2013).
It is likely that the species will be split into several species. Taxonomic work needs to be carried out on this group (ehrenbergi, leucodon and xanthodon [formerly nehringi]).

According to present taxonomic knowledge, four subspecies are distinguished by Helgen et al. 2009: S. c. citellus; S. c. gradojevici with synonyms karamani and macedonicus; S. c. istricus with synonyms laskarevi and S. c. martinoi which has balcanicus and thracius as synonyms. In a detailed revision of palearctic rodents (Kryštufek and Vohralík 2012) distinguish only three subspecies: s. c. citellus with synonyms istricus, laskarevi and probably also martinoi and balcanicus; s. c. gradojevici with synonyms thracius and macedonicus; and s. c. karamani. The validity of some subspecies should be considered as uncertain until detailed genetic studies are performed.

There are two chromosome races of this species: Spermophilus suslicus odessanus (36 chromosomes) and Spermophilus suslicus sensu stricto (34 chromosomes). These are separated by the Dnieper River. Sometimes considered as separate species, genetic and acoustic data support the integrity of both races into one species (Matrosova et al. 2016).

The species was described as Sminthus loriger von Nathusius in Nordmann, 1840, but for a long time was considered as subspecies of Sicista subtilis sensu lato (Sicista subtilis nordmanni). Now this taxon elevated to species level following Zagorodniuk and Selyunina (2009) and Cserkész et al. (2016).Sicista nordmanni (Keyserling & Blasius, 1840) is synonym as it was pointed at by Chaworth-Musters (1934). Nomenclature was revised by Zagorodniuk (2009), and current name “Sminthus loriger Nathusius in Nordmann, 1840” listed as synonym of “Sicista nordmanni Keyserling et Blasius, 1840. Sicista loriger is geographically separated from Sicista subtilis s. str. (Zagorodniuk 2011).

This species has a complicated taxonomic history which is still not entirely resolved. It is morphologically nearly indistinguishable from M. arvalis, and was therefore recognized in 1960s thanks to its distinctive karyotype (2n=54; 2n=46 in M. arvalis; see Krystufek and Shenbrot 2022).

The 2008 assessment of Cercopithecus nictitans followed the taxonomic arrangement of Grubb et al. (2003) in only recognizing two subspecies. The forms stampflii, insolitus and ludio were provisionally synonymized under the western populations of Cercopithecus nictitans martini (Grubb et al. 2003). However, it was also noted that the form on Bioko (martini) at least could have perhaps represented a distinct subspecies (J. Oates and P. Grubb pers. comm. 2008).   Oates (2011) recognised all the subspecies listed here: nictitans, martini, insolitus, ludio and stampflii and this treatment was followed in 2016. Gautier-Hion et al. (1999) recognized three subspecies: stampfli, martini and nictitans. Grubb et al. (2003) and Gautier-Hion (2013) recognised only C. n. nictitans and C. n. martini. Kingdon (2013) has recognised these subspecies as comprising Cluster II Cercopithecus nictitans cluster of the Nictitans Group. Cercopithecus n. insolitus and C. n. ludio were considered by Gautier-Hion (2013) and Kingdon (2013) to be synonyms of C. n. nictitans. Kingdon (2013) listed C. n. stampflii, but Gautier-Hion (2013) placed it as a synonym of C. n. martini.

As early as in the 1980s, taxonomic research on the ‘races’ of the genus Cebus confirmed the hypothesis that variations in the size and morphology of the tufted capuchins, could serve as important systematic and taxonomic criteria for intra-generic and intraspecific classification (Torres de Assumpção 1983, 1986; Torres 1988). Further studies completed in the last two decades have confirmed this hypothesis. According to Wallace (2008), Silva Jr. (2001, 2002) argued that the tufted and the untufted capuchins (sensu Hershkovitz 1949, 1955) are so distinct in their morphology that they should be considered a two separate genera, Cebus Erxleben, 1777 for the untufted group, and Sapajus Kerr, 1792 for the tufted capuchins. Here, the taxonomy of the tufted capuchins (sensu Hershkovitz 1949, 1955) follows Silva Jr. (2001), who did not recognize any subspecific forms. Groves (2001, 2005) presented an alternative taxonomy for the tufted capuchins as follows: C. apella apella (Linnaeus, 1758); C. apella fatuellus (Linnaeus, 1766); C. apella macrocephalus Spix, 1823; C. apella peruanus Thomas, 1901; C. apella tocantinus Lönnberg, 1939; C. apella margaritae Hollister, 1914; C. libidinosus libidinosus Spix, 1823; C. libidinosus pallidus Gray, 1866; C. libidinosus paraguayanus Fischer, 1829; C. libidinosus juruanus Lönnberg, 1939; C. nigritus nigritus (Goldfuss, 1809); C. nigritus robustus Kuhl, 1820; C. nigritus cucullatus Spix, 1823; C. xanthosternos Wied-Neuwied, 1826 (see also Fragaszy et al. 2004; Rylands et al. 2005). In this aseessment C. libidinosus paraguayanus Fischer, 1829, also listed by Groves (2001) is referred to as Cebus cay following Silva Jr. (2001).The latest information resulting from genetic studies (Lynch Alfaro et al. 2012a, 2012b) on the species of the genus Cebus confirmed the separation between tufted (robust) capuchins, and untufted (gracile) capuchins. Lynch Alfaro et al. (2012a, 2012b) thus consolidated the separation into two genera (Sapajus and Cebus) suggested earlier by Silva Jr. (2001).This assessment follows the taxonomy proposed by Rylands (2012) and Lynch Alfaro et al. (2012a, 2012b), which present the nomenclature for nine tufted capuchin monkeys: genus Sapajus (S. apella, S. macrocephalus, S. libidinosus, S. cay, S. flavius, S. nigritus nigritus, S. nigritus cucullatus, S. robustus and S. xanthosternos).  However, more recent studies that included genetic samples of S. cay from Paraguay and Brazil showed that S. cay formed a clade with S. apella and S. macrocephalus from the southwestern Amazon, to the exclusion of S. apella and S. macrocephalus from the northern Amazon (Lima et al. 2018), and that S. cay from Paraguay and southern Mato Grosso state, Brazil were genetically allied with S. apella from Rondônia state, Brazil by the Bolivian border, while S. cay from Chapada dos Guimarães, Mato Grosso formed a clade with S. apella from Alta Floresta, also in Mato Grosso state, Brazil (Lima et al. 2017). Additionally, Nieves et al. (2021) have shown that captive S. cay in facilities in Argentina show three distinct morphotypes, and that these morphotypes have a distinct geographic pattern and are related to genetic and karyotypic differences. The S. cay individuals with provenance from northwest Argentina and Bolivia were distinctively different from eastern Argentinean S. cay, and more studies are needed to better understand the diversity within this taxon (Nieves et al. 2021).

Considering molecular, morphological and biogeographic evidence, Byrne et al. (2016) proposed new genus-level systematics for the former arrangement of Callicebus species from Hershkovitz (1990): Cheracebus Byrne et al. 2016 genus for the species in the Orinoco, Negro and upper Amazon basins; Callicebus Thomas, 1903 genus for the species in the Atlantic Forest; and Plecturocebus Byrne et al. 2016 genus for the species in the Amazon basin and Chaco.Plecturocebus vieirai was described in 2012 from three localities in Pará State, Brazil (type locality: Renato River, a tributary of the right bank of the Teles Pires river, near the city of Cláudia, Mato Grosso; 11° 33' 00.15" S, 55° 10' 59.98" W) (Gualda-Barros et al. 2012), in an area formerly attributed to P. moloch sensu Hershkovitz (1990). The Vieira’s titi monkey is currently known to occur west of the Xingu River, east of the Iriri and Teles Pires rivers, southward to the headwaters of the Xingu and Teles Pires rivers, until the border between Amazonia–Cerrado biomes (Costa-Araújo et al. in press), and it is sister taxon to P. moloch (Boubli et al. 2019).

authority: Costa-Araújo, Silva-Jr., Boubli, Rossi, Hrbek & Farias, 2021
taxonomicNotes: Mico schneideri was described in 2021 for pseudo-cryptic marmosets endemic to the northern Juruena–Teles Pires interfluve, Mato Grosso State, Brazil. Marmosets from this region were stored in the Museu Paraense Emílio Goledi and known to scientists since 1995. They were, however, confounded with M. emiliae due to inadequacy of previous taxonomic assessments––entirely based on pelage colour of a few specimens––until new morphological, molecular and distribution data had shown that they are in fact morphologically diagnosable, form a fully supported clade and are allopatric, without evidence of distribution, morphological or genomic overlap with M. emiliae or another known species of Mico (Costa-Araújo et al. 2021).

Three elephant taxa remain from the sixteen elephant-like species that are known from across the planet in the Pleistocene: Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus), African Savanna Elephant (Loxodonta africana), and African Forest Elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) (Faurby and Svenning 2015, Malhi et al. 2016). The Asian and African ancestral lineages diverged approximately seven million years ago, and the African Savanna and African Forest ancestral lineages began diverging approximately one million years later (Rohland et al. 2010, Brandt et al. 2014, Roca et al. 2015, Meyer et al. 2017, Palkopoulou et al. 2018). The Third Edition of ‘Mammal Species of the World’ (Wilson and Reeder 2005) was the first to formally designate the African elephant as these two separate species. Recent genetic findings also support this designation (Roca et al. 2007, Ishida et al. 2011, Mondol et al. 2015, Palkopoulou et al. 2018, Kim and Wasser 2019). Hybridization between the two species appears restricted and evident at only 14 of the more than 100 localities recently examined across the vast forest-savanna ecotone. In nine of these 14 localities, hybrid individuals occurred alongside non-hybrid individuals of either one species or the other and not both (i.e., three localities had hybrids and African Forest Elephants only and assigned as this species; six localities had hybrids and African Savanna Elephants only and assigned as this species). For the IUCN Red List assessments, a distribution map published in Mondol et al. (2015) and recent data by Kim and Wasser (2019) are used to assign localities as range of either L. africana or L. cyclotis.

This taxon was formerly treated as a subspecies of the Macaca nemestrina group, which comprised M. n. nemestrina, M. n. leonina, and M. n. pagensis (Fooden 1975, Rosenblum et al. 1997).The boundary zone between M. leonina and M. nemestrina is not well defined and lies at the Surat Thani-Krabi depression (8-9°30'N) where ranges overlap and hybridization is likely to occur (Malaivijitnond et al. 2012). Formerly, there were reports of hybridization with M. leonina in a small area in southern mainland Thailand and on the islands of Phuket and Yao Yai (Fooden 1975, in Groves 2001), however more recent reports do not provide conclusive evidence of presence of a M. nemestrina population on Phuket (iNaturalist 2022, S. Malaivijitnond, pers. comm.). Hybridization of M. nemestrina with M. fascicularis also occurs in Sepilok, Sabah (Gilhooly et al. 2021) and is occasionally observed in other parts of Malaysia (N. Ruppert, pers. obs.).Molecular clock analysis suggests that M. nemestrina arrived in the Malay Peninsula about 0.32 million years ago; and the Bornean populations are suggested to be the first extant lineages to have separated from the other examined lineages of M. nemestrina, M. leonina, M. pagensis, and M. siberu in Southeast Asia (Abdul-Latiff and Md-Zain 2021).The population from Perak (west Peninsular Malaysia) is reported to differ genetically from other extant populations based on phylogenetic and population genetic analyses, indicating a possible subspecies distributed in the state of Perak (Abdul-Latiff and Md-Zain 2021).

There is a need for a new assessment of the European Wildcat (Felis silvestris) as it was recently recognized as a distinct species. In their revised taxonomy of the Felidae, Kitchener et al. (2017) consider Felis silvestris to comprise two subspecies, F. s. silvestris occurring in Europe, and F. s. caucasica in Anatolia and the Caucasus.However, there has been limited information on morphology and genetics of F. s. caucasica. In Turkey, F. s. silvestris (European part) and F. s. caucasica (Anatolian part), individuals are morphologically similar to each other and individual pelt patterns (spots, lines, pale or dark colouration) exhibit high diversity independent of locality, leaving no clear external morphological difference between the proposed subspecies.Several wildcat populations occurring in southern and eastern Anatolia and the Lesser Caucasus (Azerbaijan, Armenia and Iran) are F. lybica rather than F. silvestris and this situation considerably reduces the distribution of F. silvestris in Anatolia and Caucasus. A contact zone between the two species is highly possible in southern and eastern Anatolia, and the southern Caucasus (Wuest et al. 2021). Therefore, a comprehensive genetic and morphological study covering wildcat populations from eastern Europe, Anatolia and Caucasus is recommended to clarify the status and identity of wildcat populations in the region.The Afro-Asiatic wildcat (Felis lybica), also announced as a distinct species in 2017, has its own Red List assessment.The domestic cat (Felis catus) is not descended from the European Wildcat (Felis silvestris), but mostly from a lineage of the Afro-Asian wildcat (Felis lybica) from Mesopotamia (Driscoll et al. 2007). Felis silvestris was never domesticated, but it can hybridise with both Felis lybica and Felis catus.

In 2017, a taxonomic revision of all cat species recognized the split of the Leopard Cat into two different species: Mainland Leopard Cat (Prionailurus bengalensis) and Sunda Leopard Cat (Prionailurus javanensis). The Mainland Leopard Cat, meanwhile, has two recognized subspecies:Prionailurus bengalensis bengalensis in South and Southeast Asia occurring from Pakistan to China and probably inhabiting the Malay Peninsula andPrionailurus bengalensis euptilurus existing in Manchuria, Russian Far East, Taiwan, Iriomote Island and Tsushima Island.The Iriomote Cat was widely, and until recently, treated as a species. However, it is now included within the subspecies Prionailurus bengalensis euptilurus (Kitchener et al. 2017).

In Europe, the following subspecies occur: C. l. lupus (northern and eastern Europe), C. l. signatus (Iberian peninsula), and C. l. italicus (Italian peninsula, France, and Switzerland) (Sillero 2009, Wozencraft 2005).In Asia, the following subspecies occur: C. l. albus (far northern tundra Eurasia), C. l. lupus (western parts of Eurasia), C. l. pallipes (Indian subcontinent), C. l. chanco (Himalayas of India, Nepal and Bhutan and Tibetan Plateau), and C. l. arabs (Arabian peninsula) (Sillero 2009, Wozencraft 2005).In North America, the following subspecies occur: C. l. arctos (Arctic wolf), C. l. lycaon (Eastern wolf), which Chambers et al. (2012) consider a distinct species, C. l. nubilus (Plains wolf), C. l. occidentalis (Northwestern wolf or Northern Timber wolf), and C. l. baileyi (Mexican wolf) (Sillero 2009, Wozencraft 2005).In Oceania, we find the dingo, a descendant of the early east Asian dog lineage, that has taken an independent evolutionary pathway and forms a lineage that is morphologically and genetically different from grey wolves and domestic dogs. The dingo holds an important ecological and cultural role in its ecosystems. It is considered as separate and not included in this assessment.

Some studies have suggested that Sorex granarius is a sister species of Sorex araneus, whilst others argue that it occupies a basal position and should be considered the common ancestor of the S. araneus complex (see Rey et al. 2019). Regardless, although the phylogenetic position of S. granarius is currently conflictive, its taxonomic status is not.
Formerly included in S. araneus, but now recognised as a distinct species (Wilson and Reeder 2005).

Described as Tupaia tana Raffles, 1821, from Bencoolen, Sumatra. This taxon has 17 synonyms (Helgen 2005). Two subspecies are currently recognized: T. t. tana from Sumatra and its offshore islands and T. t. speciosa from Borneo and its offshore islands (Juman et al. 2021).
This taxon has four synonyms (Helgen 2005). No subspecies are currently recognized (Juman et al. 2022).

Marmota is divided into four species groups, including the caudata group which contains M. caudata and M. menzbieri. These species have been shown not to be sister species (Steppan et al. 2011). There are two recognised subspecies of M.  menzbieri (Marmota menzbieri menzbieri and Marmota menzbieri zachidovi), each subspecies has its own geographic isolate (Krystufek and Vohralik 2013). Morphological differences are slight, but relatively deep genetic divergence was reported in this species (Steppan et al. 2011).

This species was formerly included as a subspecies of Tupaia glis, until chromosomal studies by Arrighi et al. (1969) and Elliot et al. (1969) showed it to be distinct. Subsequent authors have continued to recognize this as a distinct species (Corbet and Hill 1992, Wilson 1993, Helgen 2005, Sargis et al. 2013, 2017, Hawkins 2018, Juman et al. 2022). Helgen (2005) listed 27 synonyms for this species. However, T. f. operosa Robinson and Kloss, 1914, T. f. ultima Robinson and Kloss, 1914, and T. l. kohtauensis Shamel, 1930 all have four mammae, so they should be included in T. glis (Juman et al. 2022). Similarly, we include T. glis cognata Chasen, 1940 here in T. belangeri because it has six mammae. No subspecies are currently recognized (Juman et al. 2022).

Previous records of Aethalops alecto in Borneo have been reassigned to A. aequalis (Maharadatunkamsi and Syamsul Arifin Zein 2006, Tingga and Abdullah 2012, Jayaraj et al. 2016). However, robust DNA barcodes are lacking for A. alecto across its range to determine how distinct the Peninsular Malaysia form is from that found in Sumatra and the Javan distribution forms. Additional taxonomic research is needed to determine if A. alecto represents more than a single species.

This species was assigned to the family Ptilocercidae by Shoshani and McKenna (1998), based on its possession of a number of unique external, craniodental and postcranial characters (Helgen 2005). This placement has recently been corroborated by molecular data (Janecka et al. 2007). Two subspecies are currently recognized: P. lowii lowii Gray, 1848 from Borneo and the offshore islands of Labuan and Serasan, and P. lowii continentis Thomas, 1910 from the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and the offshore islands of Bangka, Lingga, Karimunbesar, Siberut, and Pini (Helgen 2005). These subspecies exhibit some morphological divergence, and individuals from the Mentawai islands (Siberut) are craniometrically distinct from the other populations (Juman et al. 2021). Future molecular and morphological research may support the recognition of two or more species.

Sousa plumbea has been recognized as a species since taxonomic revision of the genus Sousa in 2014 (Committee on Taxonomy 2014, Jefferson and Rosenbaum 2014). Previously this species was lumped together with the Indo-Pacific Humpback Dolphin (Sousa chinensis), but animals occurring in the western part of the Indian Ocean from South Africa to western coastline of India are now recognized as taxonomically distinct from those that occur further east, based on genetics, skeletal morphology, external morphology and colour. There is uncertainty about the taxonomic affinities of the Humpback Dolphins that occur in the Bay of Bengal. Animals in this area do not appear to be S. plumbea or S. chinensis, or to be hybrids of the two, and may be a separate taxonomic entity (Amaral et al. 2017; 2020). Additional sampling should confirm the eastern limits of the S. plumbea species, but for the purposes of this assessment we assume it to be Sri Lanka and the southern tip of India in the Gulf of Mannar.

This assessment is of the revised taxonomic concept of Miniopterus schreibersii, which excludes M. fuliginosus, M. maghrebensis, M. orianae, M. pallidus and M. villiersi (all now recognised and assessed as separate species).

Haeromys minahassae is the only described species of Haeromys from Sulawesi. However, the individuals recorded from montane forests in the central core of the island may represent an undescribed species of Haeromys (Musser and Carleton 2005, Musser 2014).
This is the only representative of its genus.

Maxomys wattsi is a distinctive species that is morphologically isolated from all other Sulawesian Maxomys, except possibly M. musschenbroekii (Musser and Carleton 2005). The relationship of this species to other species in the genus should be clarified.
Represented by a small series of modern specimens from the northern peninsula, and by both modern specimens and subfossils from the southwestern peninsula of Sulawesi (Musser 1970, 1984).

This species was previously described as Paruromys and Rattus. Recent phylogenetic analyses rendered Taeromys paraphyletic with Paruromys dominator, thus, it is now recognised as Taeromys dominator. However, further phylogenetic studies are needed to determine whether Taeromys is monophyletic (Handika et al. 2021).
Further taxonomic research is needed as it is currently unclear to what extent this species differs from others in the Rattus xanthurus species group.
Further studies are required to determine whether the northern and central records are the same species (Musser and Carleton 2005).

Sody (1941) questionably included this species in Taeromys, Laurie and Hill (1954) and Musser (1984) treated it as a subspecies of Rattus xanthurus, but Musser and Holden (1991) contended that it is a distinct species most closely related to R. foramineus, which occurs in coastal lowlands of the southern end of the southwest peninsula of Sulawesi and is represented only by four modern specimens (Sody 1941) and subfossil fragments from a few localities (Musser 1984, Musser and Holden 1991).
There is a lot of morphological variation in collected specimens, though, at present, this is provisionally considered to be contained within a single species (Musser 2014).

On the northeast peninsula, Bunopmys chrysocomus is sympatric with B. fratrorum; in the central core of the island it is marginally sympatric with B. andrewsi at low elevations and B. penitus in montane forest (Musser 2014).
Synonym = R. tatei.

authority: Musser, A.S. Achmadi, Esslestyn & K.C. Rowe, 2014

taxonomicNotes: The species is closely related to Rattus hoffmanni. Further taxonomic research is needed as there is some uncertainty surrounding its status.
Prosciurillus topapuensis is a member of a species group that includes P. leucomus, P. alstoni, P. weberi, and P. rosenbergii, all endemic to Sulawesi and nearby islands (Musser et al. 2010).

Margaretamys christinae is the fourth species from the genus to be identified (M. beccarii, M. elegans and M. parvus) (Mortelliti et al. 2012). Margaretamys is a member of the Dacnomys division of Murinae (Pagès et al. 2016).
This is a distinct species distinguished from Echiothrix leucura by its shorter cranium and mandible, and shorter molar rows with simpler occlusal patterns (Musser and Carleton 2005).

Prosciurillus alstoni is a member of a species group that includes P. leucomus, P. weberi, P. topapuensis, and P. rosenbergii, all endemic to Sulawesi and nearby islands (Musser et al. 2016). On mainland Sulawesi, P. leucomus, P. alstoni, P. weberi, and P. topapuensis have allopatric ranges relative to each other.

Recent taxonomic assessments support the validity of this species. Its closest relative, based upon body size, fur colour, and craniodental morphometric traits, is P. abtrusus, which is endemic to montane forest in the Mekongga Range located on the southeastern peninsula of Sulawesi (Musser et al. 2010).
Prosciurillus weberi is a member of a species group that includes P. leucomus, P. alstoni, P. topapuensis, and P. rosenbergii, all endemic to Sulawesi and nearby islands (Musser et al. 2010).
Prosciurillus leucomus is a member of a species complex that includes P. alstoni, P. weberi, P. topapuensis, and P. rosenbergii, all endemic to Sulawesi and nearby islands (Musser et al. 2016).
Taeromys taerae is the northeast peninsular highland and morphological relative of T. hamatus, which is found only in mountains of central Sulawesi (Musser and Carleton 2005).
This species was first described by Ellerman as a subspecies of Rattus hellwaldii, but is now recognised as a distinct species.

Saiga tatarica is the only species in the genus Saiga. Two subspecies are recognised by IUCN: Saiga tatarica tatarica (to which the European and the majority of the global population belongs), and Saiga tatarica mongolica, endemic to western Mongolia. Mongolian Saiga was first described as a separate species, Saiga mongolica by Bannikov (1946) based on differences in skull measurements, shape and size of horns, and colour of pelage. However, the author later revised his opinion and considered it to be only a subspecies (Bannikov 1954).Grubb (2005) recognized the Pleistocene mammoth-steppe Saiga as a distinct species S. borealis, following Baryshnikov and Tikhonov (1994) and included the living subspecies mongolica. However, a later analysis of mtDNA from 93 tissue samples from all five extant Saiga populations confirmed that S. tatarica mongolica is genetically distinct, whereas the four populations of the nominate subspecies are polyphyletic, consistent with recent fragmentation and population declines; there were clear but only slight differences between S. t. mongolica and S. t. tatarica, confirming the designation of S. t. mongolica as a subspecies rather than a species (Kholodova et al. 2006).Campos et al. (2010) analysed modern and fossil Saiga using mtDNA from 27 ancient and 38 modern specimens from all parts of Saiga range, including two specimens of putative S. borealis. The results showed two distinct lineages, the first including all modern and fossil Saiga from north-east Yakutia and the Urals, the second occurring only in the northern Urals and now extinct. Campos et al. (2010) concluded that: “...the data suggest that S. borealis does not constitute a distinct subspecies or species”. Furthermore, the authors of this 2010 study include both Baryshnikov and Tikhonov, the co-authors of the 1994 paper, and who are therefore regarded as supporting this revised view (Mallon 2016a).Rey-Iglesia et al. (2022) sequenced the mitochondrial control region and 19 microsatellite markers of both subspecies. The result revealed low genetic diversity and low levels of heterozygosity for both S. t. mongolica (He = 0.325, Ho = 0.290) and S. t. tatarica subspecies (He = 0.215, Ho = 0.313 for Kalmykia and He = 0.274, Ho = 0.365 for Kazakhstan). The microsatellite data indicated a single population (K = 1) and therefore no structure at nuclear level between the two subspecies. This lack of genetic structure may indicate reduced time since separation of the two forms or low resolution due to the small number of S. t. tatarica samples. Increased sampling effort and a higher number of nuclear markers, ideally using genomic information, are necessary to adequately elucidate the genetic structure of the subspecies (Rey-Iglesia et al. 2022).
Records allocated to Mallomys aroaensis from the Arfak Mountains, Indonesia represent an undescribed species. Animals from the Huon Peninsula (M. a. hercules) may also represent a distinct species.

A recently published taxonomic review (Miranda et al. 2023) proposes to split the northern (in southern Bahia and Sergipe) and southern subpopulations (Espírito Santo and Rio de Janeiro) into two species - Bradypus torquatus (Bahia and Sergipe) and Bradypus crinitus (Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo), respectively. The subpopulations were already considered genetically distinct, according to previous studies (Lara-Ruiz et al. 2008, Schetino et al. 2017). This recent analysis (Miranda et al. 2023), based on coalescent delimitation using mitochondrial and nuclear DNA, morphological analyses and field observations, recognizes that they are in fact two species, B. torquatus and B. crinitus.The Maned Sloth was occasionally classified as a subgenus of Bradypus or placed in his own genus, Scaeopus (Hayssen 2009, Wetzel and Ávila-Pires 1980) due to its morphological distinctiveness. A growing number of molecular studies supports this differentiation (Gibb et al. 2016, Schetino et al. 2017, Ruiz-Garcia et al. 2020), but additional studies are needed to confirm this.
