The genus Cryptomys previously included all species now listed under the genus Fukomys (Monadjem et al. 2015). These two genera cannot be distinguished morphologically from one another, but are considered highly divergent from one another on a molecular level (Faulkes et al. 2004). Monadjem et al. (2015) lists five species belonging to the Cryptomys genus, with four of these considered endemic to the South Africa, Eswatini and Lesotho (Bennett 2013):Common Mole-rat, C. hottentotus (tentatively Northern Cape, Western Cape, Eastern Cape and Free State provinces).Natal Mole-rat, C. natalensis (tentatively KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape, Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces; Eswatini and Lesotho).Mahali Mole-rat, C. mahali (tentatively Gauteng with recent reports suggesting its extension into the Northern Cape and North-West provinces).Highveld Mole-rat, C. pretoriae (tentatively Gauteng, North West Province, possibly extending to the Limpopo River).The Matabeleland Mole-rat, C. nimrodi is not included in this assessment because it is considered a vagrant in South Africa. The southern limit of the species range is the Limpopo River and extends northwards to Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, but the eastern limit of its range is yet to be determined.In general, they are considered allopatric, however, the specific limits of each range are yet to be defined (Monadjem et al. 2015). In general, they are considered allopatric, however the specific limits of each range are yet to be defined (Monadjem et al. 2015).

This species is closely related to Habromys chinanteco and H. simulatus. However, strong morphometric differentiation and geographic isolation help to differentiate the species (Romo-Vázquez et al. 2005).

This taxon is split into separate species by some authors, including Cape Hyrax P. capensis, Abyssinian Hyrax P. habessinica, Johnston's Hyrax P. johnstoni, and Western Hyrax P. ruficeps (Hahn 1934, Kingdon 1971). Recent classifications recognize 17 subspecies. The validity of some of those is, however, ambiguous, and it is regarded here as monotypic, following more recent classifications (Olds and Shoshani 1982, Schlitter 1993, Shoshani 2005, Hoeck and Bloomer 2013).

Barbour’s Rock Mouse was formerly classified as a subspecies of Petromyscus collinus (Shortridge and Carter 1938, de Graaf 1981), but was elevated to species status by Musser and Carleton (2005), which is accepted by Monadjem et al. (2015). Although P. barbouri occur sympatrically with P. collinus, they can be comparatively distinguished by a shorter, bicoloured tail, smaller skull and shorter rostrum (Musser and Carleton 2005). Further taxonomic research is required.

Populations in Russia reviewed by Gromov and Erbajeva (1995) and Shenbrot et al. (1995). In their phylogenetic study, Gao et al. (2024) demonstrated that the continental population in China (Heilongjiang) and the island population in Russia (Sakhalin) represent two distinct evolutionary lineages showing significant genetic differentiation. Further investigation is required to determine whether the long-tailed Birch Mouse found in Heilongjiang qualifies as a new subspecies.

Rice (1998) listed two subspecies of Bearded Seals, Erignathus barbatus nauticus in the Pacific Arctic and peripheral seas and E. b. barbatus in the Atlantic Ocean and peripheral seas. This subspecies distinction has been confirmed by genetics studies (Davis et al. 2008). The ranges of the two subspecies are thought to be divided near the central Canadian Arctic in the west and the Laptev Sea in the east, with the Atlantic subspecies occurring from the central Canadian Arctic east to the central Eurasian Arctic and the Pacific subspecies occurring from the Laptev Sea east to the central Canadian Arctic, including animals in the Sea of Okhotsk (Rice 1998). Geographical variation in the calls of Bearded Seals across their range, suggests further population substructure (Risch et al. 2007) and recent whole genome sequencing and SNP analyses confirm that such additional structuring of bearded seals populations does exist (McCarthy et al. 2025). The Pacific subspecies is more homogeneous than the Atlantic subspecies, with only the Okhotsk Sea population standing out from the rest of the Beringia population in the North Pacific Arctic. Within the Atlantic there is stronger population structure with clear separation of the northwest and northeast Atlantic. Additionally, there is a discrete population in Northwest Greenland that is different from West Greenland and Canada. Bearded seals in the Svalbard Archipelago are similar to South and East Greenland.Information is lacking for Frans Josef Land and much of the North Atlantic and Central Arctic Russian territories.
Reviewed by Gromov and Erbajeva (1995) and Shenbrot et al. (1995).

Morphometric and allozyme analyses, as well as microsatellite profiling, have suggested that Hooded Seals are a single panmictic population (Wiig and Lie 1984, Sundt et al. 1994, Coltman et al. 2007). However, body size differences, behavioural differences and the breeding site fidelity displayed by populations, make further genetics investigations warranted. Currently, management is conducted for two regions (Sergeant 1974, Lavigne and Kovacs 1988): 1) the Northwest Atlantic group, which has traditionally given birth in three areas - Davis Strait, the southern Gulf of St Lawrence and off of northeastern Newfoundland (an area known as the “Front”), Canada, and 2) Hooded Seals from the Northeast Atlantic that breed on ice east of Greenland, in the Greenland Sea, northwest of the island of Jan Mayen (Rice 1998).
This species is sometimes inappropriately referred to as coxingi.

Formerly included in the genus Gazella, Dama Gazelle is now assigned to the genus Nanger, along with Soemmering’s Gazelle N. soemmerringi and Grant’s Gazelle N. granti following Groves (2000) and Grubb (2005).Several Dama Gazelle subspecies have been described, based on variations in pelage patterns. Cano (1984) recognized three subspecies that were provisionally retained by Scholte (2013). These were described from a small number of specimens obtained from different parts of the range. Those in the east have a larger amount of white on the hindquarters and a reduced or no brown haunch stripe; the amount of chestnut-brown increases towards the west and the stripe on the haunches becomes larger and more prominent. Analysis of mitochondrial DNA sequences revealed no genetic support for this 3-subspecies arrangement (Senn et al. 2014, 2016). It is not known if the variation in colour has any adaptive variation or if it represents an east-west cline – there are extensive geographic gaps in sampling across the range. There are also no clear natural barriers to limit movements of individuals, and therefore gene flow, between different parts of the range (Senn et al. 2014). Dama Gazelles have three different chromosome numbers (n = 38, 39, 40) which also do not align with the three named subspecies. In addition, wild herds may show variation in appearance, especially in the centre of the range, demonstrated by photos of wild groups containing different phenotypes and Dama Gazelles portrayed in rock art in southern and western Algeria that are also relatively pale and more similar to eastern forms (Lamarque et al. 2007a,b; RZSS and ASG 2014). A thorough review of historical descriptions, colour patterns, taxonomic arrangements, rock art and other evidence is provided by Kitchener (2018). Only the species is assessed here.

The scientific name for the Harp Seal has shifted frequently with generic names including Pagophoca, Pagophilis and Phoca, and specific names being either groenlandicus or groenlandica. Berta and Churchill (2011) returned to the name Pagophilus groenlandicus; this is the name currently recognized by the Society of Marine Mammalogy.Rice (1998) recognized two Harp Seal subspecies, P. g. groenlandicus and P. g. oceanicus, the former breeding in the western North Atlantic off North America and also around Jan Mayen in the Greenland Sea, and the latter breeding in the White Sea. But, there are mixed genetic findings and no consensus on the subspecies issue. Many studies have explored the relationships between animals from the three breeding groups. All studies have found distinctions, although the relative degrees of differentiation among the groups differ according to the methodology used (Yablokov and Sergeant 1963, Heptner et al. 1996, Meisfjord and Sundt 1996, Rice 1998, Perry et al. 2000, Carr et al. 2015). Animals from the Greenland Sea and the White Sea overlap extensively during summer foraging migrations (Folkov et al. 2004, Nørdøy et al. 2008), but they return to their respective breeding grounds (Oien and Øritsland1995). So it is the current convention to describe populations only according to their three distinct breeding areas: 1) off the east coast of Canada, both in the Gulf of St Lawrence and northeast of Newfoundland in an area known as “the Front”; 2) in the Greenland Sea, northwest of Jan Mayen Island, which traditionally has been called “the West Ice”; and 3) in the White Sea, which has traditionally been referred to as “the East Ice”.

This species has been confused other species of Crocidura such as C. russula but is recognised as a distinct species on the basis of a cranial morphometrics analysis as clarified by Jiang and Hoffmann (2001).
Significant genetic differences noted by Cserkész et al. (2019) lead to the description of the Zhetysu Alatau population of Sicista tianschanica as a new species: S. zhetysuica.

Based on genetic analyses, true R. losea is probably only distributed in Cambodia, Viet Nam and south eastern China and Taiwan, with other distribution records corresponding to other taxa (K. Aplin pers. comm.).

Taxonomy currently used by the IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group (see Kitchener et al. 2017): Panthera leo leo—Central Africa, West Africa and Asia Panthera leo melanochaita—Southern and East Africa Lions were previously described as two subspecies: the African Lion (Panthera leo leo) and the Asiatic Lion (Panthera leo persica). However, recent studies (Bertola et al. 2015, 2016, 2022) indicate that lions in Western and Central Africa are more closely related to lions found in India than to those found in Southern and East Africa. This is likely the result of lions being reduced to local refugia during the more recent part of the Pleistocene climatic cycles (Bertola et al. 2011, 2016). Divergence times estimated from genetic data match large-scale changes in habitat, including expansion and contraction of forested areas, possibly reducing connectivity and isolating lion populations (Bertola et al. 2016). This temporary isolation may have led to divergence of populations, which can still be observed today. Historical connectivity between lion populations in West or Central Africa and populations in India explain the close evolutionary relationships between these populations, even though a series of bottlenecks have caused the Indian population to differentiate quickly as a result of increased genetic drift (Bertola et al. 2015, 2016, 2021, 2022). According to recent genetic studies, Ethiopia is identified as a suture zone for lion populations, indicating significant genetic overlap between P. l. leo and P. l. melanochaita (Bertola et al. 2021). This suture zone putatively includes Dinder National Park in Sudan, Boma and Badingilo National Parks and Kidepo Game Reserve in South Sudan, and all lion populations across Ethiopia and Kidepo Valley National Park in Uganda (Bertola et al. 2021; Bertola et al. in prep.). This zone is a natural occurrence and was not created through species or area management, and there is no intention to intervene to reduce or prevent hybridization from occurring between the two subspecies. See Table 1 in the Supplementary Information for supporting information regarding population subspecies classification.

In the past, the Galápagos Sea Lion was considered a subspecies of the California Sea Lion Z. californianus (Z. c. wollebaeki). However, Rice (1998) argued for the retention of Z. wollebaeki as distinct species. Recent genetic data support the classification as a separate species that became isolated from the California Sea Lion about 2.3 ± 0.5 million years ago (Wolf et al. 2007). This status has recently been confirmed further by mitochondrial genome data (Austin et al. 2023). Lopes et al. (2021) Genome-wide sequencing showed that Z. wollebaeki is a sister taxon to both Z. californianus and Eumetopias jubatus (Steller Sea Lion) and that Z. wollebaeki diverged from the others as recently as 0.25 million years, with the three-species group diverging from the other eared seals as early as 5.4 million years ago (Lopes et al. 2021).

Originally described as a separate species, it was next considered to be a geographic population or a subspecies of S. giganteus as its morphological traits did not reach the 'species level' (Ognev 1947, Topachevskiy 1969). It was then re-evaluated back to separate species based on minor morphological differences (Puzachenko 1993). Taxonomic status needs to be reassessed based on genetic markers.
Populations from India and southeast Asia may represent different taxa and further studies are needed to resolve this (D. Lunde pers. comm.).

Recent molecular and morphological work has identified three clades within Dromiciops that were given the names gliroides, bozinovici, and mondaca D'Elía et al. 2016). There have been numerous studies since 2016, when bozinovici and mondaca were described, both in support and opposition to the recognition of these three species based on various lines of evidence (Valladares-Gómez et al. 2017, Martin 2018, Suárez-Villota et al. 2018, Quintero-Galvis et al. 2022); the most recent of these based on genomic sequence data suggested a two species model, treating bozinovici and gliroides as species and mondaca as a subspecies of gliroides (Quintero-Galvis et al. 2022). The latter is the arrangement followed here, although the systematics of Dromiciops is in considerable flux.

Recent molecular and morphological work has identified three clades within Dromiciops that were given the names gliroides, bozinovici, and mondaca D'Elía et al. 2016). There have been numerous studies since 2016, when bozinovici and mondaca were described, both in support and opposition to the recognition of these three species based on various lines of evidence (Valladares-Gómez et al. 2017, Martin 2018, Suárez-Villota, et al. 2018, Quintero-Galvis et al. 2022); the most recent of these based on genomic sequence data suggested a two species model, treating bozinovici and gliroides as species and mondaca as a subspecies of gliroides (Quintero-Galvis et al. 2022). The latter is the arrangement followed here, although the systematics of Dromiciops is in considerable flux.
This species is monotypic. It forms a monophyletic group with Cryptotis goldmani and Cryptotis peregrinus (Guevara and Cervantes 2014).

Cryptotis goodwini and probably Cryptotis griseoventris are sister species. However, genetic studies to test this hypothesis are lacking (Guevara 2023). Cryptotis goodwini are larger in size; however, cranial measurements of the species broadly overlap (Woodman 2010).
This taxon was previously considered a subspecies of Cryptotis parvus, but has been elevated to species status (Hutterer 2005). This species is monotypic (Alvarez-Castañeda 2024).

authority: Monadjem, Kerbis Peterhans, Nalikka, Waswa, Demos & B.D. Patterson, 2020
taxonomicNotes: The species was described based on the holotype collected immediately adjacent to the Mabira Forest Reserve, Mukono District of the Central Region, Uganda in October 2012. A male paratype was captured in the same area and on the same night, exhibiting close genetic and morphological resemblance to the holotype (Monadjem et al. 2021).

Wozencraft (2005) regarded this species as conspecific with the congeneric Congo Clawless Otter (Aonyx congicus). The two are here retained as distinct species (see van Zyll de Jong 1972, Wozencraft 1993, Somers and Nel 2013). Coetzee (1977) recognised three subspecies A. c. capensis (including coombsi and angolae), from southern Africa, W Zambia, Angola, Gabon, Nigeria and throughout West Africa; A. c. hindei (including helios), from Uganda to E DR Congo as far south as N Zambia; and A. c. meneleki, from Ethiopia.

While this species was included in the genus Lutra by, amongst others, Koepfli and Wayne (1998), recent molecular research places it in the genus Hydrictis Pocock, 1921 (Koepfli et al. 2008, Sato et al. 2012), and has been included as such in d’Inzillo Carranza and Rowe-Rowe (2013). Five subspecies have been recognised from across the continent (Meester et al. 1986) but further research is needed to confirm the validity of these.
Peromyscus caniceps was previously considered a subspecies of P. fraterculus (Hafner et al. 2001), but evidence suggests it should retain full species status (Cornejo-Latorre et al. 2017).

Peromyscus dickeyi was previously considered a subspecies of Peromyscus merriami (Hafner et al. 2001),  but evidence suggests it should retain full species status (Cornejo-Latorre et al. 2017). This species is monotypic (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).

Taxonomic confusion in that some believe that Peromyscus gymnotis is actually just a small P. mexicanus. However, P. gymnotis appears to be a distinct species (Pérez-Montes et al. 2023), though may only be restricted to the foothills of the Chiapas and northern Guatemala (Hernández-Canchola et al. 2022).
This species is monotypic (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024)
This species may be split in two, with the original species corresponding to the region near Rio Cojones (SMSG 2018).
This monotypic species is part of the Peromyscus boylii complex (Álvarez-Castañeda 2024).
Peromyscus sagax is supported as a valid species (Tiemann-Boege et al. 2000). This is a monotypic species (Cruzado 2014).
Split from Peromyscus boylii (Bradley et al. 2004).

Taxonomy is currently under review by the IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group. Johnson et al. (2006) and Eizirik et al. (2008) placed yagouaroundi in the genus Puma. However, Agnarsson et al. (2010) noted that the Jaguarundi is not a sister species to the Puma. More recently Segura et al. (2013) looked at cranial development within the Puma clade and found that while this is similar in Cheetah and Puma, but that of the Jaguarundi is quite different. Given these phylogenetic uncertainties, and these and other morphological and behavioural differences, the IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group retains this species in Herpailurus (Kitchener et al. 2017).
Previously included in Uropsilus gracilis, but separated based on form and distribution (Smith and Xie 2008).

For many years this taxon was known only from the type locality, and another location close by in southern Gansu (Hoffman 1987). Several additional specimens have now been taken in southwest Gansu, Qinghai, Shaanxi, east Xizang, Sichuan, and Yunnan (Smith and Xie 2008, Song et al. 2021, Huang et al. 2022, Zhu et al. 2024). Molecular evidence demonstrated a distinct lineage in the Gansu specimens which morphologically align with the original description of this species, therefore supporting the separate species status of Sorex cansulus (Bannikova et al. 2018).
It has been confirmed as a separate species from Sorex buchariensis using nuclear analysis (Bannikova et al. 2018).

Euroscaptor kuznetsovi used to be considered part of Euroscaptor longirostris, but was separated by considering DNA sequence data and multivariate analysis of cranial characters of the two (Zemlemerova et al. 2016).
This species was previously assigned to Crocidura nimbae (Hutterer 2005).

Previously recognised as belonging to a monotypic genus Oreailurus, primarily based on the relative size difference in the skull's auditory chambers obtained from very few specimens (Cabrera 1940, Wozencraft 1993, Nowell and Jackson 1996, Yensen and Seymour 2000). Subsequently, based on genetic evidence, the Andean Cat was included in the genus Leopardus. The specific name, jacobita, is in honour of Jacobita Mantagazza (Cornalia 1865) and should not be declined to jacobitus as is sometimes seen in the literature (Sanderson 2015).

Based on morphological analysis, Khorozyan et al. (2006) recognize Panthera pardus tulliana (Valenciennes, 1856) in western Türkiye and P. p. sindica (Pocock, 1930) in Pakistan, and possibly also parts of Afghanistan and Iran. They also consider P. p. ciscaucasica (Satunin, 1914) as the senior synonym for P. p. saxicolor.Kitchener et al. (2017) in their revised taxonomy of the Felidae recognize the following eight Leopard subspecies:Panthera pardus pardus (Linnaeus, 1758): Africa.Panthera pardus tulliana (Valenciennes, 1856; 1039): Türkiye, Caucasus, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan and Pakistan.Panthera pardus fusca (Meyer, 1794): Indian subcontinent, Burma and China.Panthera pardus kotiya Deraniyagala, 1949: Sri Lanka.Panthera pardus delacouri Pocock, 1930b: Southeast Asia and probably southern China.Panthera paruds orientalis (Schlegel, 1857) including japonensis: Eastern Asia from Russian Far East to China.Panthera pardus melas (Cuvier, 1809; 152): Java.Panthera pardus nimr (Hemprich and Ehrenberg, 1832): Arabian Peninsula.The treatment by Kitchener et al. (2017) is followed by the IUCN Red List.

Until recently, two species were recognised in the genus Delphinus: the Short-beaked Common Dolphin (D. delphis) and the Long-beaked Common Dolphin (D. capensis), as described by Heyning and Perrin (1994). The morphological differences between D. delphis and D. capensis in the North Pacific (Heyning and Perrin 1994) were supported by molecular evidence from both mitochondrial and nuclear markers (Rosel et al. 1994). However, the genus exhibits a great deal of morphological variation globally and the criteria used to distinguish between the two species in the North Pacific appear not to apply elsewhere (Best 2007). In South Africa, Samaai et al. (2005) found that based on skull morphology the majority of specimens belonged to D. capensis, however, two specimens were within the range for D. delphis from the North Pacific, and a third specimen fell between the ranges for D. delphis and D. capensis (Samaai et al. 2005). The same molecular markers that were used to differentiate the two sympatric species in the North Pacific failed to reveal any genetic distinction between the described morphotypes in South Africa (Best 2007).Subsequently, Cunha et al. (2015), in a global analysis of Delphinus which included nine specimens from the west coast of South Africa (eastern South Atlantic), concluded that all specimens analysed from the Atlantic Ocean belonged to D. delphis, and that D. capensis was not a genetically valid species.In 2016 the Society for Marine Mammalogy Committee on Taxonomy removed Delphinus capensis from its accepted list of marine mammal species and now recognises all Common Dolphins globally as belonging to a single species, Delphinus delphis (Committee on Taxonomy 2020). It recognises the following subspecies:D. d. delphis Linnaeus, 1758. Common Dolphin D. d. bairdii Dall, 1873. Eastern North Pacific Long-beaked Common Dolphin D. d. ponticus Barabash, 1935. Black Sea Common Dolphin D. d. tropicalis van Bree, 1971. Indo-Pacific Common Dolphin Cunha et al. (2015) noted that because the sympatric or parapatric Long-beaked and Short-beaked Common Dolphins off California in the eastern North Pacific appear not to interbreed, the Long-beaked Common Dolphins might eventually be described and recognised as a separate species, D. bairdii. Some researchers have considered the Long-beaked Common Dolphins in the Indo-Pacific, which has an exceptionally long beak, to constitute a separate species, D. tropicalis (Van Bree and Gallagher 1978, Rice 1998). However, another morphometric study concluded that that form should be considered a subspecies (Jefferson and Van Waerebeek 2002) and it is currently recognised as such, D. delphis tropicalis.The non-concordance of morphological and genetic data for Common Dolphins has caused much confusion and a rigorous global taxonomic study of the genus is needed. Further phylogenetic analyses are necessary to resolve the controversies surrounding the classification and nomenclature. More changes to Delphinus taxonomy should be expected.
Three subspecies are recognised: M. p. prehensilis (mainland Cuba), Mysateles p. gundlachi (North Isla de la Juventud), and M. p. meridionalis (South Isla de la Juventud) (Turvey et al. 2017).

Based on the work of Woods et al. (2001), Woods and Kilpatrick (2005, p. 1596)  argued that "Mysateles was paraphyletic and that the affinities of melanurus are with taxa of the genus Mesocapromys rather than with Mysateles". This designation is not widely accepted (e.g., Silva Taboada et al. 2007), hence this species is treated here under Mysateles.

authority: Chen Zhongzheng, He Kai, Huang Cheng, Wan Tao, Lin Liangkong, Liu Shaoying, & Jiang Xuelong, 2017
taxonomicNotes: Chodsigoa hoffmanni was previously included in Chodsigoa parca (Lunde et al. 2003, He et al. 2010). Based on molecular and morphological evidence, it is now recognised as a separate species (Chen et al. 2017).
Originally described as a subspecies of Chodsigoa smithii (Anthony 1941) and then as a subspecies of Chodsigoa parca (Hoffmann 1985), but is now recognised as a separate species (Chen et al. 2017).

Chodsigoa parca used to include Chodsigoa furva (Allen 1923, Hoffmann 1985), and was reported to include Chodsigoa hoffmanni (Lunde et al. 2003). However, based on molecular and morphological evidence, Chodsigoa hoffmanni is now recognised as a separate species (Chen et al. 2017). Chodsigoa parca currently includes the subspecies Chodsigoa parca parca and Chodsigoa parca lowei, which is only known from a single specimen, suggesting the relationship needs to be addressed (Chen et al. 2017).
Capra walie is here treated as a distinct species from Capra ibex and Capra nubiana, following Grubb (2005), see also Gebremedhin et al. (2009).

Genus Scotophilus Leach, 1821 was reviewed by Trujillo et al. (2009) and Demos et al. (2018). Scotophilus celebensis was suggested to be a synonym by Tate (1942) and Sinha (1980), and this was confirmed in a genus-level review by Tu et al. (2021).

The taxonomic relationship between Arctocephalus philippii and Arctocephalus townsendi has been debated extensively. The debate has included whether the two species are conspecific (Repenning et al. 1971), as well as whether both species should be in a separate genus from Arctocephalus (Arctophoca; Sivertsen 1954, Brunner 2004) or remain within this genus, but as distinct species. Genetic evidence from Nyakatura and Bininda-Emonds (2012) suggests that both species should be in the genus Arctocephalus until further research is conducted.Mitochondrial DNA suggests that A. philippii and A. townsendi are distinct species (Wynen et al. 2001, Higdon et al. 2007). However, the whole issue of appropriate thresholds for mtDNA divergence required to establish solid genetic evidence for species separation continues to be discussed. Arctocephalus philippii remains the current official taxonomic name of the Juan Fernandez Fur Seal (Society for Marine Mammalogy, Taxonomy Committee 2024).

The taxonomy of the Grey Seal, Halichoerus grypus, is confusing. Bonner (1981) concluded that there are three populations isolated both geographically and by timing of reproduction. Chapskii (1975) recognized the three populations as separate subspecies, H. g. grypus in the western North Atlantic, H. g. atlantica in the eastern North Atlantic, and H. g. baltica in the Baltic Sea.Rice (1998) recognized two subspecies, H. g. grypus in the western and eastern North Atlantic and H. g. macrorynchus in the Baltic Sea. However, Boskovic et al. (1996) analyzing mtDNA and McCarthy et al. (2025) analyzing nuclear DNA, found large differences between the three breeding areas. In both analyses, Baltic and East Atlantic populations were found to be much closer to one another than they were to the west Atlantic population. The Society for Marine Mammalogy recognizes two subspecies, the Western Atlantic Grey Seal (H. g. grypus) and the Eastern Atlantic Grey Seal (H. g. macrorynchus) (Committee on Taxonomy 2025). The IUCN Pinniped Specialist Group prefers the common names Northwest Atlantic Grey Seal and Northeast Atlantic Grey Seal, and in the past has assessed those subspecies separately. This assessment evaluates the overall Red List status for H. grypus globally.

Morphological, reproductive and behavioural differences separate Spotted Seals from their close relatives, the North Pacific Harbour Seals (Phoca vitulina richardii and P. v. stejnegeri) both of whose ranges overlap with the Spotted Seal (Rice 1998). Recent studies of mtDNA confirmed the distinctiveness of the Harbour and Spotted Seals at the species level. The two species have hybridized in captivity, although information on hybrids occurring in the wild is limited to one possible case (O’Corry-Crowe and Westlake 1997). While Shaughnessy and Fay (1977) identified several separate breeding concentrations, the initial, small, genetic samples did not show geographic substructure within the species (O’Corry-Crowe and Westlake 1997). More recent analyses of larger samples indicate possible population structure between the Yellow Sea, the Sea of Okhotsk, and the Bering Sea (Boveng et al. 2009, O’Corry-Crowe and Bonin 2009, Li et al. 2010).

Historically, two subspecies have been described (Meester et al. 1986). Felis nigripes nigripes, the nominate genotype form described by Burchell, was first described near Kuruman in the Northern Cape, South Africa. Its range includes present-day southeastern Namibia, parts of Botswana, South Africa in the Northern Cape, North West, Gauteng, Limpopo and marginally into Mpumalanga provinces. Felis nigripes thomasi (Shortridge 1931) was described from a specimen collected near Grahamstown in the Eastern Cape. Its range includes the present-day Eastern Cape, westwards to the southern regions of the Northern Cape and the Free State. However, other, more recent sources indicate that these findings are spurious and that the species is monotypic (Smithers 1971, Olbricht and Sliwa 1997, Kitchener et al. 2017). In addition, no isolating geological events (i.e., glaciation, large rivers during the Last Glacial Maximum) occurred that would have sufficiently isolated the above-mentioned populations to deserve subspecies designation.Fortunately, unlike the Afro-Asiatic Wildcat (Felis lybica), this species does not hybridize easily with other cat species. The only confirmed hybrid cases (Black-footed Cats and domestic Cats) were under captive conditions (Leyhausen 1979). None have been recorded from the wild (A. Sliwa and B. Wilson pers. obs. 2025).
This species has a strong sister group relationship with Habromys chicanteco (Rogers et al. 2007).

This species was previously considered monotypic (Castro-Campillo et al. 2014), but recent analysis suggests it contains at least two subspecies (Peromyscus furvus angustirostris and P. f. furvus) and likely two additional species (Cruz-Gómez et al. 2021).

This species has traditionally either been included in the genus Felis (Kral and Zima, 1980) or Profelis (Pocock 1917, Wozencraft 2005). More recent molecular data unequivocally reveal that the African Golden Cat belongs to the Caracal lineage, together with the Caracal (Caracal caracal) and the Serval (Leptailurus serval; Johnson et al. 2006). The divergence time between the Caracal and the African Golden Cat would be situated between 6 and 5 Ma (Zhou et al. 2017). The African Golden Cat is not closely related to the Asiatic Golden Cat (Catopuma temminckii; as it may be assumed). There might be two subspecies separated by the Dahomey Gap that divides the Upper from the Lower Guinean Forest (i.e., West Africa from the rest of the species range; Smithers 1968, Van Mesch and van Bree 1969) but genetic studies are needed to confirm or refute this (Kitchener et al. 2017).
Two subspecies are recognised: Zygogeomys trichopus tarascensis and Zygogeomys trichopus trichopus (Hafner and Barkley 1984).
This species is now recognised under a new genus, Xerospermophilus (Helgen et al. 2009).
This taxon was returned to specific rank by Carleton et al. (2002). It has a similar morphology to Habromys lepturus (Rogers et al. 2007).
There is a disagreement whether or not three subspecies of Sciurus arizonensis should be recognised. This species is monotypic (Koprowski et al. 2016).

taxonomicNotes: Three elephant taxa remain from the sixteen elephant-like species that are known from across the planet in the Pleistocene: Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus), African Savanna Elephant (Loxodonta africana), and African Forest Elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) (Faurby and Svenning 2015, Malhi et al. 2016). The Asian and African ancestral lineages diverged approximately seven million years ago, and the African Savanna and African Forest ancestral lineages began diverging approximately one million years later (Rohland et al. 2010, Brandt et al. 2014, Roca et al. 2015, Meyer et al. 2017, Palkopoulou et al. 2018). The Third Edition of ‘Mammal Species of the World’ (Wilson and Reeder 2005) was the first to formally designate the African elephant as these two separate species; the IUCN followed in 2021 (Hart et al. 2021). Genetic evidence supports the designation (Roca et al. 2007, Ishida et al. 2011, Mondol et al. 2015, Palkopoulou et al. 2018, Kuhner et al. 2025). Hybridisation between the two species appears to be rare: it was evident in less than 7% of nearly 2,500 individuals and 19 of 118 localities sampled across the forest-savanna ecotone and beyond (Kuhner et al. 2025). In 15 of the 19 localities where hybrids were identified, both hybrid and non-hybrid individuals were found alongside each other, where the non-hybrids were of either one species or the other and not both (i.e., nine localities had hybrids and African Forest Elephants only and assigned as this species; six localities had hybrids and African Savanna Elephants only and assigned as that species) (Kuhner et al. 2025). For the IUCN Red List assessments, localities are categorised by species type according to the criteria described and assignments made in the most recent species status report published by the IUCN (Maisels et al. 2025).

Antarctic Fur Seals were initially divided into two groups (Wynen et al. 2000), a western group in the South Atlantic region of the Southern Ocean, including populations at South Georgia, South Shetland Islands, South Sandwich Islands, and Bouvetøya (southwest to central south Atlantic) and a group in East Antarctica, including both the Indian and Southwest Pacific Ocean sectors. It is hypothesised that this latter group might have expanded from a refugial population found on the Kerguelen Islands after the last glacial maximum (Cleary et al. 2021). Modern breeding colonies from this second group are located at Marion and Prince Edward Islands, the Kerguelen Islands, the Crozet Islands, Heard and McDonald Islands and Macquarie Island. A reassembly of the species genome (Humble et al. 2018) still identifies the eastern group as a single subpopulation but separates South Georgia, South Shetland Islands and Bouvetøya into different subpopulations (see Paijmans et al. 2020). The genetic identity of breeders at the South Sandwich Islands, in the Scotia Sea and west of South Georgia, remains unknown but is likely the same as South Georgia (given its proximity).Antarctic Fur Seals are very similar to other southern fur seals, particularly the females, and hybridisation is common. This is probably a result of the recent evolution of Antarctic Fur Seals, which has taken place in the past 2–3 million years (Yonezawa et al. 2009). Hybrids between Antarctic Fur Seals and Subantarctic Fur Seals (Arctocephalus tropicalis) have been reported at Macquarie Island (Lancaster et al. 2006), Marion Island (Hofmeyr et al. 2006) and Crozet Island (Kingston and Gwilliam 2007). At Macquarie Island, female Antarctic Fur Seals have also hybridised with New Zealand Fur Seal males (Arctocephalus forsteri) (Lancaster et al. 2006, Goldsworthy et al. 2009). There is some degree of reproductive success in hybrids (Lancaster et al. 2006).

California Sea Lions were once considered a subspecies of Zalophus californianus (Z. c. californianus) by many authors, but Rice (1998) argued that Z. californianus, Z. japonicus, and Z. wollebaeki are distinct species. Other studies have confirmed the separate species status of Z. japonicus and Z. californianus (Brunner 2004, Sakahira and Niimi 2007) and the separation of Z. californianus and Z. wollebaeki (Wolf et al. 2007).
Rice (1998) states that the correct spelling of the specific name is carcinophaga, not the once widely used carcinophagus. He provides a discussion of the history of this issue.

Leopardus geoffroyi (d’Orbigny and Gervais, 1844) was initially classified under the genera Felis and Oncifelis before being reassigned to the genus Leopardus (Johnson et al. 2006). While earlier proposals suggested the recognition of four subspecies (Wozencraft 2005, Ximenez 1975), these classifications are not supported by recent morphological (Nascimento 2014) and genetic studies (Johnson et al. 1999, Goméz Fernández et al. 2020, Bou et al. 2021). Instead, the species shows a geographical cline, leading the IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group to recognise it as a monotypic species in its latest assessment (Kitchener et al. 2017). A recent study identified two distinct genetic clusters within the species, one in the north-northeast and the other in the south-southwest of its range (Fameli et al. 2024). These clusters exhibited moderate gene flow, with differences in dispersal patterns and genetic diversity between them. The species' phylogeographic origin has been traced to central Argentina (Fernández et al. 2020).Lescroart et al. (2023) proposed dividing the genus Leopardus into three subgenera to better define its main subclades, with one subgenus now being Oncifelis. As a result, the full current name of Geoffroy’s cat is Leopardus (Oncifelis) geoffroyi. In southern Brazil, a hybrid zone has been documented where the northern range of L. geoffroyi overlaps with the southernmost range of Leopardus guttulus (Trigo et al. 2008, 2013). This hybridization was first suggested by disrupted phenotypes observed in the contact zone (Eizirik et al. 2006) and later confirmed through molecular data (Trigo et al. 2008, 2013).
